title: Long-term chromatin accessibility tracking after a transient stimulus
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a defined pulse of an AP-1-activating stimulus such as TPA, wounding cytokines, or inflammatory signals. After withdrawal, run time-course ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag for Fos/Jun, and H3K27ac profiling to see whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist for days to weeks after AP-1 activity returns to baseline.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation or dominant-negative block during vs. after priming
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) c-Jun/Fos or inducible dominant-negative A-Fos to remove AP-1 either during priming or after the memory state is established. Then measure the secondary-challenge transcriptional response. If the memory needs AP-1 only for establishment, it is epigenetically self-sustaining. If it needs AP-1 for maintenance, AP-1 is the ongoing carrier of memory.

title: Single-cell multiome linking AP-1 motif accessibility to response history
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC (or lineage-barcoded clones) on primed and naive populations, before and after re-stimulation. Test whether cells with persistent AP-1 motif accessibility, inferred by chromVAR or footprinting, respond faster or more strongly, and whether the state is inherited by sister cells through division.

title: Sufficiency of AP-1 activity using optogenetic or chemogenetic control
description: Drive AP-1 factors with light-inducible or drug-inducible systems using different durations, dynamics, and dosages (pulsed vs sustained). Test whether AP-1 activity alone is sufficient to install lasting accessibility and enhanced re-response at target loci, using reporter lines at AP-1-regulated enhancers to read out the memory in live cells.

title: Site-specific perturbation of memory enhancers and cooperating factors
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 or motif mutation at candidate AP-1-dependent memory enhancers, and pioneer-factor or chromatin-remodeler (e.g., BAF) loss, to test whether the sites are necessary for faster re-induction of nearby genes. Pair this with Hi-C or Micro-C and histone-mark profiling to determine whether AP-1 maintains memory directly or by recruiting other chromatin regulators.

title: Long-term tracking of AP-1-bound enhancers after a transient stimulus
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a defined pulse of AP-1-activating signal (TPA, TNF, wounding, or stress). Then run time-course ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for JUN/FOS, H3K27ac, and H3K4me1 after washout, to test whether AP-1-bound enhancers stay open and occupied well after the stimulus and AP-1 activity have returned to baseline.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 after priming (necessity for maintenance vs. establishment)
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS, JUN, or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS. Deplete AP-1 either during the priming pulse or only after it, then re-challenge the cells. If memory is maintained by AP-1 itself, post-priming depletion should erase the primed state. If AP-1 only establishes memory, then only depletion during priming should do so.

title: Secondary-stimulus recall assay with single-cell readouts
description: Compare primed and naive cells for transcriptional response magnitude and kinetics to a second stimulus using scRNA-seq, live-cell reporters, or smFISH of AP-1 target genes. Quantify how long the heightened response persists and whether it is inherited through cell divisions, using lineage tracing or sister-cell comparisons.

title: Live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and a feedback-loop model
description: Track endogenously tagged FOS/JUN levels, activity reporters, and target-gene transcription in single cells across stimulation histories. Fit mathematical models to test whether positive feedback (e.g., JUN autoregulation) or a pioneer-like chromatin-opening mechanism produces bistability and hysteresis, and test the model's predictions by perturbing feedback nodes.

title: Targeted enhancer perturbation and sufficiency tests
description: Use CRISPR to delete or mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers. Use dCas9-based tethering of AP-1 or chromatin modifiers to test sufficiency, and use in vivo models (e.g., skin inflammatory memory, wound re-epithelialization) to ask whether motif-specific loss abolishes faster recall of the response. Together, these experiments distinguish AP-1 as a causal memory element from AP-1 binding that merely correlates with memory.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus such as serum, TPA, or injury cues. Run time-resolved ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 (FOS/JUN) and H3K27ac over days to weeks after washout; persistence of AP-1 motif-enriched accessible sites after the stimulus ends would indicate a lasting memory-like state.

title: Acute degron depletion at defined time windows
description: Use auxin-inducible degron or dTAG alleles of FOS, JUN, or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 during priming, during the memory phase, or at re-stimulation. Compare the secondary response across these windows; AP-1 required only at priming versus continuously separates initiation from maintenance roles.

title: Re-stimulation response assay (primed vs naive)
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then give a second stimulus. Measure transcription (nascent RNA-seq/PRO-seq), the kinetics, and the amplitude of target genes relative to naive cells. Test whether the enhanced or faster response is tied to AP-1-bound loci, and whether it is lost on AP-1 perturbation or on blocking enhancer opening.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Apply single-cell RNA plus ATAC (multiome) with barcode lineage tracing or live imaging of AP-1 reporters to follow primed cells through divisions. Test whether AP-1 occupancy or accessibility is inherited by daughter cells and whether it predicts clonal differences in later responses. This separates heritable memory from persistent signaling and measures its stability across cell cycles.

title: Targeted locus perturbation and synthetic AP-1 memory test
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 to silence or edit AP-1 motifs at specific memory-associated enhancers. Separately, use optogenetically or chemically inducible AP-1 (e.g., inducible FOS/JUN) to drive a pulse of AP-1 activity at synthetic reporter loci. Test whether the motif is necessary for the primed state, and whether AP-1 activity alone, independent of upstream signaling, is sufficient to create a lasting accessible state and a faster response.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., PMA, TNF, or injury signals), then wash out and perform time-resolved ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 (FOS/JUN) and H3K27ac across days to weeks. Persistence of AP-1-dependent accessible sites after AP-1 activity returns to baseline, versus naive controls, would indicate a memory-like state.

title: Acute degron-based AP-1 depletion at different time points
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degradation of FOS or JUN, or a dominant-negative (A-FOS), to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or after it has ended. If depletion after priming erases the enhanced secondary response, AP-1 is needed to maintain memory; if only depletion during priming matters, AP-1 is needed for initiation but not maintenance.

title: Secondary-stimulation transcriptional response assays
description: Compare RNA-seq (bulk and single-cell) of primed versus unprimed cells after a second challenge, and link faster or stronger induction of genes to AP-1-bound, pre-opened enhancers. Quantify memory with a response-ratio metric and test dependence on AP-1 motif integrity via CRISPR editing or MPRA of primed-state enhancers.

title: Single-cell multiome and live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics
description: Use paired scRNA/scATAC-seq and live imaging of AP-1 activity reporters (e.g., FOS-GFP knock-in, AP-1 motif reporters) to track whether individual cells retain heritable AP-1-linked accessibility states through divisions. Lineage tracing or sister-cell comparisons would distinguish cell-autonomous, mitotically heritable memory from population-level selection or persistent paracrine signaling.

title: Sufficiency test via synthetic AP-1 recruitment and in vivo validation
description: Use dCas9-based or optogenetic recruitment of AP-1 factors (or pioneer-like AP-1 with BAF) to naive loci, then test whether transient recruitment alone creates stable accessibility and enhanced responsiveness after removal. Complement this with in vivo models (e.g., wound healing, inflammation, or neuronal activity) to check whether AP-1 occupancy patterns predict persistent states in tissue, with controls for continuing signals.

title: Long-term tracking of chromatin accessibility after a transient stimulus
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a defined AP-1-activating stimulus such as TPA, anisomycin or an inflammatory cue, then wash it out. Perform time-course ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN, FOSL) over days to weeks to test whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after AP-1 binding and activity return to baseline.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) JUN/FOS or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) system to remove AP-1 at different times after the priming stimulus. If accessibility and the enhanced secondary transcriptional response persist after AP-1 loss, AP-1 is an initiator. If they collapse, it is a continuous maintainer.

title: Primed re-stimulation response assays
description: Prime, rest, and re-stimulate cells, then compare transcription (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) and kinetics of AP-1 target genes with naive cells. Test whether memory depends on AP-1 motifs by comparing wild-type with CRISPR-mutated motifs at selected enhancers, and by AP-1 inhibition during priming only.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Use scATAC/RNA multiome with barcoded lineage tracing or live AP-1 reporters (e.g., FOS-GFP) to follow sister cells through divisions after transient stimulation. Quantify whether accessibility and expression states are heritable across divisions, and whether they are bimodal or stable per clone, beyond what random cell-to-cell variation would produce.

title: Mechanistic dissection of chromatin features and cofactors at memory sites
description: At sites that stay open after priming, profile H3K27ac, H3K4me1, SWI/SNF (BAF) occupancy and pioneer factors with CUT&Tag. Then perturb BAF (e.g., BRG1 inhibitors) or deposit/remove marks with dCas9 tools to test whether AP-1 maintains memory through chromatin remodeling or histone modification. Compare with DNA methylation and with non-AP-1 sites as controls.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells to a defined, transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, wounding cues, or PMA). Then perform time-resolved ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN across days to weeks after withdrawal. Test whether newly opened AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay open after AP-1 binding itself has decayed, which would indicate memory.

title: Re-stimulation (primed) response assay with AP-1 dependence
description: Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) of naive versus previously stimulated cells upon a second challenge. Include acute AP-1 loss of function (dominant-negative A-FOS, degron-tagged FOS/JUN) either during the first stimulus only or during the second only. This separates the role of AP-1 in establishing memory from its role in executing the memory response.

title: Optogenetic or chemogenetic AP-1 pulse-chase
description: Drive AP-1 activity with a light- or drug-inducible JUN/FOS construct with controlled pulse duration, amplitude, and frequency. Measure how persistence of target gene expression and enhancer state depends on input dose and dynamics, to determine whether AP-1 alone is sufficient to establish a self-sustaining state and whether a threshold exists.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Use single-cell RNA plus ATAC, with barcoded lineage tracing, to follow stimulated cells and their daughters through divisions. Quantify whether sister cells share AP-1 target accessibility and expression more than unrelated cells. Combine with live imaging of AP-1 reporters to check for heritable states that persist through mitosis.

title: Chromatin mechanism dissection: pioneer activity, histone marks and feedback loops
description: Map the histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1), BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment and DNA methylation at AP-1 sites before, during and after stimulus. Mutate or CRISPR-edit specific AP-1 motifs, and use dCas9 epigenetic editors to test necessity. Also test positive feedback (e.g., JUN autoregulation) with perturbation and mathematical modeling to see whether it yields bistable, heritable states.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a defined, transient stimulus (serum, TNF, wounding cue) and perform time-course ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 (FOS/JUN), H3K27ac and H3K4me1 through days to weeks after washout. Persistent accessible sites containing AP-1 motifs, and enhanced re-induction of nearby genes upon restimulation, would indicate AP-1-based memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation or inhibition during priming versus maintenance
description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or only after it, then test the recall response. If AP-1 is needed only for establishing memory, the memory is chromatin-encoded; if it is needed for maintenance, AP-1 itself carries the memory.

title: Single-cell multiome and live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and memory heterogeneity
description: Pair single-cell RNA+ATAC-seq with live reporters (e.g., FOS-GFP, AP-1 activity reporter) in primed vs. naive cells to link AP-1 history (amplitude, duration) to later accessibility and transcriptional response. Lineage tracing through divisions would test whether the memory is heritable and bistable versus graded and decaying.

title: Sufficiency test with synthetic or optogenetic AP-1 activation and locus-specific editing
description: Induce AP-1 with optogenetic or chemically inducible FOS/JUN pulses of varied dose and duration, and use dCas9-based recruitment or CRISPR motif mutation at selected enhancers. Test whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to open chromatin and create a stable, restimulation-responsive state, and which sites require it.

title: Mapping AP-1 cooperativity with chromatin remodelers and histone marks
description: Perform ChIP/CUT&Tag and proteomics for AP-1 interaction with BAF (SWI/SNF) components, plus BAF inhibition or depletion, and footprinting/Micro-C to assess nucleosome remodeling and looping at memory loci. Testing whether remodeler loss erases persistence despite AP-1 re-binding clarifies the mechanistic link between AP-1 and epigenetic memory.

title: Persistence of AP-1-associated chromatin accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a defined pulse of AP-1-activating stimulus (TPA, TNF, injury), then withdraw it and track ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN and H3K27ac at multiple time points. Persistent AP-1 motif-enriched accessible sites after signaling returns to baseline, together with a faster or stronger transcriptional response to restimulation, would indicate memory.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 factors during and after the priming window
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) on FOS, JUN, or ATF family members to remove AP-1 only during priming, only during the memory/maintenance phase, or only at restimulation. If depletion during priming blocks memory but depletion afterward does not, AP-1 is needed for establishment. If depletion afterward erases memory, AP-1 is also required for maintenance.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of lineage-linked memory
description: Perform paired scRNA/scATAC-seq, or live imaging of AP-1 reporters, on clonally barcoded cells before priming, after priming, and through divisions. This tests whether AP-1 activity states and accessible regions are heritable across cell divisions, and whether they predict each clone's response to restimulation beyond what noise would explain.

title: Pioneer-like function and chromatin-state causality at AP-1 sites
description: Use CUT&RUN or ChIP for AP-1, SWI/SNF (BAF) and histone marks, combined with perturbations such as BAF inhibition or CRISPR base-editing of motifs at specific memory enhancers. Test whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient to open chromatin and keep it accessible after the signal ends, and whether the marks are lost when AP-1 is removed.

title: Synthetic AP-1 activation with dose, duration, and feedback modeling
description: Drive AP-1 activity with optogenetic or chemogenetic inputs of varying amplitude, duration, and frequency, then measure the lasting output (target gene expression, accessibility) after input removal. Fit dynamical models to test for bistability, hysteresis, or positive feedback (e.g., FOS/JUN autoregulation) as the mechanism, and compare with AP-1-independent controls.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and FOS/JUN binding at multiple time points after a transient stimulus (e.g., wounding, inflammation, or stress) and long after stimulus withdrawal. Persistent AP-1-motif-associated accessible sites would indicate a memory-like epigenetic state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation/inhibition during priming vs. recall
description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or dominant-negative A-FOS/T-5224 to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only after it has been withdrawn, then measure the secondary response. Distinguishing a role in establishing versus maintaining memory shows whether AP-1 is required for the memory itself.

title: Single-cell multiome analysis of memory-state heterogeneity
description: Perform paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq on primed and naive cells to link AP-1 motif accessibility and target-gene expression to the strength of the secondary response. Use lineage barcoding to test whether the state is inherited through cell divisions.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics across repeated stimulation
description: Image endogenously tagged JUN/FOS or AP-1 transcriptional reporters in single cells across repeated stimulus pulses and across lineages. Measuring persistence, hysteresis, and heritability of the signal over days would test for memory-like dynamics.

title: Pioneer-like activity and histone modification analysis at AP-1 sites
description: Test whether AP-1 binding deposits or maintains H3K27ac/H3K4me1 and recruits BAF at primed enhancers, and whether these marks persist after AP-1 is lost. Combine ChIP-seq, CRISPR motif mutation, and enhancer reporter assays to show causality.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag of AP-1 footprints after transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at timepoints after a transient stimulus and long after its withdrawal. Persistent AP-1-dependent open sites that outlast the signal would indicate a memory-like state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) tools to remove AP-1 after the stimulus is gone. Then measure whether accessibility and the secondary-response transcriptional boost are lost, which would show AP-1 is needed to maintain memory rather than just to establish it.

title: Re-stimulation assays with RNA-seq
description: Compare transcriptional responses in naive versus previously stimulated cells after a rest interval of varying length. Test whether faster or stronger induction of target genes depends on AP-1 levels and occupancy.

title: Single-cell multiome and live imaging of AP-1 dynamics
description: Use single-cell RNA+ATAC, or live reporters of FOS/JUN, to follow lineages and test whether the AP-1 state is inherited through divisions and is bistable. This separates heritable memory from transient signaling.

title: Targeted AP-1 site perturbation with CRISPR deletion or dCas9 repression and histone-mark profiling
description: Use CRISPR deletion or dCas9-based repression of specific AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers. Profile H3K27ac and H3K4me1 to test whether AP-1 binding is causally required for persistent enhancer marks and for the memory response at linked genes.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after a transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at timepoints during and long after a transient stimulus (e.g., wounding, inflammation, stress) to see whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after the signal is gone and AP-1 levels have returned to baseline.

title: Secondary challenge (priming) assays with AP-1 perturbation
description: Expose cells to a first stimulus, rest them, then re-stimulate and measure transcriptional response magnitude/kinetics by RNA-seq; compare with AP-1 dominant-negative (A-FOS), CRISPRi, or degron cells to test whether AP-1 is required for faster or stronger memory responses.

title: Timed acute AP-1 degradation to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Use inducible degrons (dTAG/auxin) on FOS/JUN to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or after memory is established. Then assay whether memory-associated accessibility and gene expression persist without AP-1, to distinguish an initiating role from a maintaining role.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Perform single-cell RNA+ATAC with lineage barcodes or live-cell AP-1 reporters to test whether AP-1 activity state and its chromatin footprint are inherited through cell divisions and correlate with heterogeneous memory responses among sister cells.

title: Histone mark and SWI/SNF (BAF) dependence at AP-1 sites
description: Measure H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and BAF occupancy at AP-1 motif-containing enhancers before, during, and after stimulation. Use BAF inhibitors or enhancer motif mutation/dCas9 editing to test whether these marks and AP-1-driven chromatin opening are necessary and sufficient for persistence.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and FOS/JUN binding before, during, and long after a transient stimulus (e.g., injury, inflammation, or stress). Test whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after the stimulus is withdrawn and AP-1 protein has returned to baseline.

title: Secondary challenge (priming) assay with AP-1 perturbation
description: Expose cells to a first stimulus, rest them, then re-stimulate and measure the faster or stronger transcriptional response. Use inducible dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS), CRISPRi, or degron systems at different times to show whether AP-1 is required for establishing versus maintaining the memory.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage tracing of memory states
description: Perform paired scRNA/ATAC-seq on clonally related cells to determine whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target gene expression states are heritably transmitted through divisions, and whether they predict future response heterogeneity.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity dynamics
description: Track AP-1 activity using fluorescent reporters or tagged FOS/JUN in single cells over days and across divisions to measure persistence, bistability, and positive feedback (e.g., c-Jun autoregulation), and relate past activity history to current state.

title: Epigenetic mark and pioneer-factor mechanistic dissection
description: Combine ChIP/CUT&Tag for histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1), BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment, and DNA methylation with AP-1 motif mutation or site-specific dCas9 editing at memory enhancers to test if AP-1 is necessary and sufficient to establish stable, self-sustaining chromatin states.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at timepoints during and long after a transient stimulus (e.g., wounding, inflammation, stress) to see whether AP-1-dependent open regions persist after the signal has ended and AP-1 levels have returned to baseline.

title: Secondary challenge (priming) assays with AP-1 perturbation
description: Expose cells to a first stimulus, rest them, then re-stimulate and measure faster or stronger transcriptional responses. Test whether inhibiting or degrading AP-1 (dominant-negative A-FOS, dTAG/degron) during priming only, versus during recall only, abolishes the memory.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of memory-state heterogeneity
description: Use scRNA+ATAC with lineage barcoding to determine whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target-gene expression define stable, heritable cell states that persist through cell divisions and predict future responsiveness.

title: Live-cell imaging of AP-1 dynamics and reporters
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or AP-1 reporters over days in single cells and lineages to measure pulse dynamics, persistence, and inheritance by daughter cells, correlating history with subsequent response.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and sufficiency tests at AP-1 sites
description: Use CRISPR deletion of AP-1 motifs or dCas9-based editing at memory enhancers, plus ectopic AP-1 induction, to test whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient to establish lasting accessibility, histone marks (H3K27ac), and enhanced re-induction, including pioneer-factor and BAF-complex dependence.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at timepoints during and long after a transient stimulus (e.g., inflammation, injury, stress) to identify sites that stay open after AP-1 levels return to baseline. Persistence of accessibility at AP-1 motif sites indicates memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Use inducible degradation (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS either during priming or after the stimulus has ended. If the memory response persists when AP-1 is removed after priming, AP-1 is only an initiator; if it is lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain memory.

title: Re-stimulation assays measuring faster or stronger transcriptional response
description: Prime cells, rest them for days to weeks, then restimulate and measure nascent transcription (PRO-seq/RNA-seq) and AP-1 recruitment kinetics versus naive cells. Test whether the enhanced response depends on AP-1-bound primed enhancers by CRISPR perturbation of the motifs.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of AP-1 activity and heritability through divisions
description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC, or live reporters of AP-1 activity, with lineage tracing to see whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells. Quantify the persistence of the state, its bimodality, and its dependence on cell division.

title: Histone modification and chromatin remodeler co-profiling at AP-1 sites
description: Measure H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and BAF/SWI-SNF occupancy at AP-1 sites, and test whether inhibiting the remodeler or the modifying enzyme erases the memory. This tests whether AP-1 stores memory through epigenetic marks rather than its own continued presence.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at time points after a transient stimulus and long after its withdrawal. Persistently open AP-1 motif-containing enhancers would indicate a retained memory state.

title: Re-stimulation (primed vs. naive) transcriptional response assays
description: Expose cells to a first stimulus, rest them, then re-stimulate and measure target gene induction by RNA-seq or qPCR. Faster or stronger induction in primed cells compared with naive ones, and its loss on AP-1 inhibition, would test whether AP-1 is required for memory.

title: Acute AP-1 perturbation during priming vs. recall
description: Disrupt AP-1 with a dominant-negative such as A-FOS, an auxin degron on JUN/FOS, or CRISPRi, either only during the priming phase or only during recall. This separates the role of AP-1 in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage tracing or live reporters
description: Use single-cell RNA+ATAC, or live AP-1 activity reporters tracked through cell divisions, to determine whether the memory state is inherited by daughter cells. Test for heterogeneity and bistability in AP-1 activity and accessibility.

title: Pioneer-factor and chromatin-state analysis at memory loci
description: Combine histone modification profiling (H3K27ac, H3K4me1), BAF/SWI-SNF occupancy, and DNA methylation with CRISPR or base-editing mutation of AP-1 motifs. This tests whether AP-1 sites are causally required to keep enhancers primed, and whether memory persists once AP-1 itself is lost.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and FOS/JUN binding at timepoints during and long after a transient stimulus (e.g., injury, inflammation, or stress) to test whether AP-1-dependent open regions persist after the signal is gone. Compare with naive cells to identify a lasting memory signature.

title: Acute AP-1 perturbation during priming versus recall
description: Use dominant-negative A-FOS, CRISPRi, or degron systems to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only at re-stimulation. If memory requires AP-1 for establishment and/or maintenance, the secondary response should be lost differentially, separating the two roles.

title: Primed re-stimulation transcriptional response assays
description: Stimulate cells twice with a rest interval and measure faster or stronger induction of target genes (RNA-seq, nascent RNA/PRO-seq) relative to first-exposure cells. Correlate enhanced responses with AP-1 motif-containing loci to link memory phenotype to AP-1.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of AP-1 activity and lineage inheritance
description: Combine single-cell RNA/ATAC with lineage barcoding or live-cell AP-1 reporters to determine whether AP-1 activity states are inherited through cell divisions and heterogeneous across clones. Persistence across divisions without ongoing signal would support memory.

title: Synthetic AP-1 induction sufficiency test with histone-mark readouts
description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic pulses of FOS/JUN expression to test whether AP-1 alone is sufficient to create persistent enhancer accessibility, H3K27ac/H3K4me1 marks and memory-like responses. Pair this with BAF/chromatin-remodeler inhibition to test the mechanism.

title: Hysteresis loop mapping of AP-1 activity vs. stimulus
description: Ramp a controllable input (e.g., optogenetic or chemically induced ERK/JNK signaling, or inducible c-Fos/c-Jun) up and then down, and measure single-cell AP-1 reporter output and target-gene expression. A path-dependent loop, with different up and down thresholds that persist after the stimulus is removed, would indicate bistability. Memory would then be a property of the system's stable states rather than a lingering signal.

title: Bimodality and critical slowing down near the threshold
description: Tune stimulus dose or AP-1 abundance toward the putative tipping point and track single-cell time series with live reporters. Look for rising variance and autocorrelation time, diverging relaxation time after perturbation, and a shift from unimodal to bimodal distributions. These are generic signatures of a nearby bifurcation and would show whether AP-1 sits close to a transition.

title: Perturbation and relaxation test of state stability
description: Deliver pulses of varying amplitude and duration, then knock AP-1 down transiently (degron, dominant-negative) or overexpress it, and record whether cells return to the original state or settle into a new one. Mapping the fraction of cells in each state as a function of perturbation size defines the boundaries between states. Persistence after the perturbation is cleared, and its dependence on feedback loops such as FOS/JUN autoregulation, would distinguish a self-sustaining stable-state memory from slow decay.

title: Time-resolved ATAC/CUT&Tag with AP-1 motif tracking
description: Profile accessibility, AP-1 occupancy and histone marks at AP-1-bound enhancers before, during and long after transient stimulation, including after cell divisions. Test whether enhancers opened by AP-1 stay open once AP-1 returns to baseline, and whether they enable faster or stronger re-induction. Pair this with AP-1 degradation at different times after the stimulus to distinguish initiation from maintenance of the memory.

title: Inference of a landscape and dynamical model from single-cell data
description: Combine single-cell RNA-seq or multiome data with live reporters to fit a stochastic dynamical model (e.g., Langevin or Fokker-Planck) of AP-1 and its targets. Estimate the effective potential, number of minima, barrier heights and Kramers-type switching rates, then test the model's predictions of how memory lifetime scales with noise, feedback strength and AP-1 dosage experimentally.

title: Mutual information between past stimulus and present AP-1 state
description: Deliver defined stimulus histories (e.g., varied EGF/ERK pulse number, amplitude, duration) and measure single-cell AP-1 state (live FOS/JUN reporters plus chromatin accessibility at AP-1 motifs) at increasing delays after stimulus withdrawal. Estimate the mutual information I(stimulus history; AP-1 state) in bits versus delay; memory is supported if information persists well beyond the lifetime of upstream signaling and FOS/JUN transcript/protein, and the decay time constant gives the memory half-life.

title: Channel capacity of AP-1 signaling with and without chromatin feedback
description: Treat ERK/JNK dynamics as input and AP-1 target-gene output (nascent RNA, enhancer accessibility) as output, and estimate channel capacity from single-cell dose-response and dynamic-input distributions. Compare wild type with perturbations (dominant-negative A-FOS, BAF/SWI-SNF inhibition, degron-tagged JUN) to test whether AP-1-dependent chromatin remodeling increases capacity or the number of distinguishable stored states beyond what transient transcription alone allows.

title: Acute AP-1 removal after priming to test whether the primed state is self-sustaining
description: After a priming stimulus, rapidly degrade or inhibit AP-1 (dTAG/AID on FOS/JUN, or A-FOS induction) at varied times and measure whether primed enhancer accessibility, H3K27ac, and the enhanced re-response persist. Quantify the conditional entropy of the secondary response given priming, with and without continued AP-1. AP-1-maintained memory should lose information upon removal, whereas AP-1-initiated but chromatin-held memory should persist, separating initiation from maintenance.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance across divisions
description: Use barcode lineage tracing with paired scATAC/scRNA to compare AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression between sister cells and cousins after priming. Compute mutual information between mother and daughter states over generations and compare to shuffled controls; high, slowly decaying inter-generational mutual information at AP-1 sites indicates heritable memory, with the per-division loss of information as the rate of memory loss.

title: CRISPR motif editing and optogenetic activation to test sufficiency and coding structure
description: Optogenetically drive FOS/JUN (or specific dimer compositions) with programmed pulse patterns and, separately, mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers via base editing. Measure whether transient AP-1 activation alone produces a lasting state, whether different dimer/dynamic patterns yield distinguishable stored states (decoding accuracy, confusion matrix, bits per cell), and whether motif loss abolishes the stored information at that locus.

title: Hysteresis mapping by ramping AP-1 input up and down
description: Use optogenetic or chemically inducible control of AP-1 (e.g., c-Fos/c-Jun, or upstream JNK/ERK), sweep the input up and then down, and measure single-cell AP-1 activity and target-gene output. A bistable memory element would show hysteresis, meaning different on and off thresholds and path-dependent output at identical input; a monostable system would not.

title: Pulse-duration and frequency stimulation with washout
description: Deliver defined stimulus pulses varying in amplitude, duration, and spacing, and track AP-1 reporter dynamics and chromatin accessibility for hours to days after washout. Fit linear and nonlinear state-space models to estimate decay time constants and test whether the system retains a state after input removal, and test whether a prior pulse alters the response to a later one (priming), which would indicate memory beyond the stimulus.

title: Perturbing AP-1 feedback loops
description: AP-1 autoregulates (c-Jun induces its own transcription, and Fos/Jun feed back on DUSPs and other negative regulators). Open each loop using CRISPRi on the c-Jun promoter, dominant-negative TAM67, or a synthetic constitutive replacement of the endogenous promoter. Then test whether memory is lost, which would show the loop is necessary. Add a synthetic positive feedback to test whether it is sufficient to create memory in naive cells.

title: Single-cell live imaging with lineage tracking and state estimation
description: Image endogenously tagged Fos/Jun (or AP-1 reporters) in single cells over multiple divisions after transient stimulation. Quantify heritability of the state across mother-daughter pairs, bimodality, and switching rates, and apply observer/Kalman-style state estimation to the reporter time series to infer hidden states such as chromatin-bound AP-1 versus nuclear abundance. This tests whether the hidden state is observable and persistent.

title: Chromatin-level readout of the stored state (ATAC/CUT&Tag/Hi-C time courses)
description: After transient stimulation, profile AP-1 motif accessibility, AP-1 occupancy, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at enhancers over time, comparing naive, primed, and recovered cells. Then perturb AP-1 binding acutely, for example with degron-tagged Jun or Fos, at different delays after the stimulus. If memory is stored in the enhancer state and needs AP-1 to be maintained, late removal should erase it; if AP-1 only establishes the state, late removal should leave it intact, which separates establishing from maintaining roles.

title: Transient-stimulus hysteresis assay with chromatin accessibility readout
description: Expose cells to a defined, brief AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., serum, TPA, or stress), wash out, and track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN) and ATAC-seq accessibility over days to weeks. Memory is supported if AP-1-dependent enhancers stay open and primed after TF levels return to baseline, and if a second challenge gives a faster or stronger transcriptional response than the first, indicating path-dependence.

title: Acute degradation and optogenetic AP-1 pulses to test necessity and sufficiency
description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) during priming, during the memory window, or at recall to test whether AP-1 is needed to establish versus maintain the memory. Pair this with optogenetic or chemogenetic AP-1 pulses of varied duration, amplitude and frequency to map the relationship between input and memory, and test whether AP-1 activation alone can write the state.

title: Single-cell lineage-resolved memory and heritability measurements
description: Combine live-cell AP-1 reporters with lineage tracing or barcoding and multiome (scRNA and scATAC) to measure how long the primed state persists across divisions and how correlated it is between sister cells. Compare decay time and heritability with the noise-driven state fluctuations expected without memory, to separate true epigenetic memory from fixed cell-state differences or clonal selection.

title: Enhancer-level mutational scanning of the memory landscape
description: Run saturating mutagenesis or CRISPR-edited variants of AP-1 motifs (TRE sites) and their spacing or cooperative partners at primed enhancers, using a reporter that records the response to the first and second stimulus. This identifies which motif sequence and arrangement features set memory strength, how robust the memory is to mutation, and whether the trade-offs between sensitivity, memory persistence and noise are constrained.

title: Comparative evolutionary analysis of AP-1 memory sites
description: Compare AP-1-primed enhancers across mammals or other lineages with ATAC, ChIP and conservation scores, and test whether motif turnover and constraint are stronger at sites showing memory than at sites showing transient responses. Add population-level variant data (eQTL/caQTL) to test whether memory-linked elements are under purifying selection, which would show that memory has fitness value. Examine trade-offs such as faster re-response against the cost of maladaptive persistence in chronic inflammation or cancer.

title: Priming dose-response and hysteresis analysis
description: Prime cells with a graded range of AP-1 activating stimuli (e.g., PMA, TNF, anisomycin, or optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun induction), wash out, then challenge with a fixed second stimulus after varying delays. Plot the secondary response against the priming dose and the washout interval to obtain EC50 shifts, Emax changes, and memory decay half-lives, with hysteresis and a persistent left-shift of the dose-response curve as the signature of memory.

title: Time-windowed AP-1 inhibition with concentration-response curves
description: Apply a selective AP-1 inhibitor (e.g., T-5224 or dominant-negative A-Fos) during priming only, the rest period only, or the challenge only. Run full concentration-response curves, and include inactive analogs and off-target controls for selectivity. If memory requires AP-1 during the rest period, it is actively maintained rather than only set at priming; the difference between memory-specific and acute-response IC50s defines the window.

title: Longitudinal profiling of chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy
description: Use ATAC-seq or CUT&RUN for c-Jun, c-Fos, and H3K27ac at multiple times after stimulus washout. Look for AP-1 motif-containing enhancers that stay open after the stimulus is gone and respond faster or more strongly on restimulation. Correlate the persistence of each site with the magnitude of the recall response per locus, as a quantitative readout of memory.

title: Single-cell reporter tracking of bistability and heritability
description: Use live-cell AP-1 reporters or endogenous tagged Fos/Jun to follow single cells and their lineages through priming, rest and rechallenge. Measure whether the primed state is all-or-none and whether it passes through divisions. Dose-response curves with a sharp, switch-like Hill coefficient and bimodal distributions would support a self-sustaining memory circuit over a graded carryover.

title: Synergy analysis of AP-1 with co-regulators and epigenetic modifiers
description: Test combinations of AP-1 perturbation with inhibitors of chromatin regulators (BAF/SWI-SNF, p300, HDACs, DNMTs) in a dose-matrix. Analyze with Bliss and Loewe synergy models to see whether they act in the same pathway for memory maintenance. Synergy or antagonism patterns, plus Jun/Fos paralog-specific knockdown, help place AP-1 as an initiator, maintainer, or reader of memory.

title: Transient-stimulus intervention with acute degron removal at different times
description: Define memory as an effect of past exposure (S_t0) on later response (R_t1) after the stimulus has ended, with AP-1 binding/chromatin accessibility as the mediator. Deliver a pulse (e.g., TNF, EGF, or optogenetic ERK), then use a dTAG/AID degron to remove FOS/JUN either before the pulse, during the memory window, or only at restimulation. If memory persists when AP-1 is removed after the pulse, AP-1 isn't required for maintenance. If it vanishes, AP-1 is necessary. This separates establishment from maintenance.

title: Mediation analysis with single-cell multiome and lineage-tracked cells
description: Run paired scRNA+scATAC (or CUT&Tag) on clonally barcoded cells before and after priming and restimulation. Estimate natural direct and indirect effects of priming on secondary transcription through AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR), adjusting for cell cycle, cell state, and clone as confounders. Use sibling-cell concordance within clones to separate heritable memory from shared microenvironment, and add sensitivity analyses (E-values) for unmeasured confounding of the mediator–outcome link.

title: Locus-specific causal perturbation of AP-1 sites with CRISPR editing and dCas9 tools
description: Mutate or CRISPRi/dCas9-block AP-1 motifs at selected primed enhancers, or tether a dominant-negative (A-FOS) there, then test whether the faster or stronger secondary response is lost at that gene only. Compare against matched control motifs to rule out off-target accessibility effects. This yields site-level interventional evidence, rather than correlational ChIP, and tests whether memory is cis-encoded.

title: Positive-feedback and bistability test via synthetic circuits and mathematical modeling
description: Memory mechanisms predict hysteresis and self-sustaining states. Quantify AP-1 (FOS/JUN) levels with live reporters across a dose-ramp up and down, and test for path dependence, bimodality, and decay time. Then cut candidate feedback edges, such as the JUN autoregulation promoter or the AP-1–BAF/p300 accessibility loop, in the DAG-informed model to see which edges are necessary for persistence. Fit competing models, including AP-1-independent ones like histone-mark memory, and compare them with held-out perturbations.

title: Genetic variation and cell-type contrasts as instruments for AP-1 occupancy
description: Use allele-specific analysis of AP-1 motif-altering variants (caQTL/ASE in heterozygous cells, or MPRA) as instruments for AP-1 occupancy, and test whether the allele with stronger binding retains accessibility better and shows a greater secondary response after stimulus withdrawal. Also compare contexts with different priming histories, such as trained immunity or senescence, using difference-in-differences on accessibility between primed and naive states, to obtain within-individual evidence that is robust to confounders.

title: Persistence of AP-1 state after stimulus removal
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or wounding), then withdraw it and track AP-1 factor composition (FOS/JUN family), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and re-challenge transcriptional response over days to weeks. Memory is defined as a post-stimulus state that differs from the naive state and shows a faster or larger response, or dependence on stimulus history.

title: AP-1 family composition and diversity indices across time and cell states
description: Use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) and CUT&RUN or ChIP for each FOS/JUN/ATF member to quantify the relative abundance of AP-1 dimers at enhancers. Compute Shannon/Simpson diversity and beta-diversity (turnover) of AP-1 composition between naive, stimulated, and recovered cells to test whether a persistent shift in composition marks memory.

title: Competition between AP-1 and other factors at shared enhancers
description: Map footprinting and motif occupancy of AP-1 relative to competing factors (e.g., CTCF, lineage TFs, NF-κB, glucocorticoid receptor) at memory-associated enhancers, and perturb AP-1 dosage using a degron or dominant-negative (A-FOS) to see whether the sites are lost or occupied by other factors. Displacement of AP-1 by other factors, or their gain of occupancy on AP-1 loss, would show whether AP-1 holds the site open and excludes competitors, thereby maintaining memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degron removal after the priming window
description: Deplete AP-1 (dTAG/auxin degron on FOS or JUN, or A-FOS) either during priming or only during the memory interval, then re-stimulate. If memory persists after AP-1 loss in the interval, AP-1 is only an initiator. If it collapses, AP-1 actively maintains memory. Pair this with ATAC-seq and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) to separate chromatin-based from TF-based persistence.

title: Lineage-tracked single-cell heritability and mathematical modeling of state persistence
description: Use barcoded lineage tracing or live reporters (AP-1 activity reporter, FOS-GFP) to measure whether AP-1 state is inherited across divisions or reset by noise, comparing sister-cell correlation to random pairs. Fit bistability or positive-feedback population models to estimate persistence half-life, and test predictions by perturbing feedback loops such as FOS/JUN autoregulation.

title: Hysteresis and bistability test of path-dependence
description: Expose cells to graded doses of a transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., PMA, stress, or optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun), then measure AP-1 target accessibility and expression after washout. Hysteresis, bimodal single-cell distributions, and a persistent high state under identical final conditions would indicate multiple stable states, which would indicate memory rather than a transient response.

title: Time-resolved ATAC/CUT&Tag of AP-1 occupancy through stimulus and washout
description: Measure chromatin accessibility, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at defined time points after a stimulus ends. Test whether AP-1 sites stay open and primed, and whether loci that carry memory are enriched for AP-1 motifs relative to matched controls.

title: Necessity and sufficiency via acute degradation and optogenetic timing
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS) to remove AP-1 during priming, during the memory interval, or at re-challenge, and optogenetically pulse AP-1 in naive cells. Comparing the effects of depletion at each stage (for example, loss of memory only when AP-1 is depleted during priming) separates AP-1 roles in establishing, maintaining, or reading out memory.

title: Re-stimulation response assay with single-cell readouts
description: Apply a first and second stimulus separated by variable delays, and measure the speed, amplitude, and cell-to-cell variability of transcriptional response (scRNA-seq, live reporters) versus naive cells. Fit decay kinetics of the primed advantage to estimate memory half-life, and test whether it depends on AP-1 dosage or motif integrity.

title: AP-1 motif perturbation and feedback-loop modeling
description: Edit AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers with CRISPR base editing, or run a massively parallel reporter assay, to test whether memory is locus-intrinsic. In parallel, build a dynamical model with AP-1 positive autoregulation (c-Jun autoinduction) and chromatin feedback, fit it to the data, and test whether it predicts when memory is stable, using inhibition of feedback components as the falsification step.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells to a brief inflammatory or stress stimulus (e.g., TNF, wound signal), then run ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at multiple time points, including days to weeks after withdrawal. Persistent AP-1-motif-enriched accessible regions after the signal is gone would indicate AP-1-dependent memory, and these can be compared to naive cells.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined times
description: Use an inducible degron (e.g., dTAG on c-JUN/FOS) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or after it has ended. If AP-1 is needed only for establishment, depletion during priming abolishes memory; if it is needed for maintenance, depletion after priming erases it. This separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Re-stimulation response assay with enhancer-level readouts
description: Prime cells, rest them, then restimulate and measure faster or stronger transcription (nascent RNA-seq such as PRO-seq, or scRNA-seq) at AP-1-bound loci versus unprimed controls. Pair this with H3K27ac and chromatin accessibility profiling to link a heightened response to AP-1-marked enhancers, and test whether CRISPR mutation of AP-1 binding sites removes the effect.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Combine single-cell ATAC and RNA with lineage barcodes or sister-cell pairing to test whether AP-1 activity states and accessibility are inherited through divisions. High sister-cell concordance that persists after the signal ends, and that exceeds what current AP-1 levels explain, supports epigenetic heritability rather than ongoing signaling.

title: Live-cell AP-1 dynamics and synthetic locus perturbation
description: Image AP-1 reporters or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN with single-molecule tracking over days, measuring bimodality and persistence of activity after transient input. Also use optogenetic or dCas9-based recruitment of AP-1 (or its motif deletion) at a reporter locus to test whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to create a self-sustaining active state, and whether that depends on cofactors like BAF/SWI-SNF or histone marks.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or T cells) to a defined stimulus such as TPA, TNF, or TCR signaling, then wash out and rest for days to weeks. Re-challenge them and compare transcriptional kinetics and amplitude with naive cells by RNA-seq, to test whether a persistent, AP-1-dependent altered response exists.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 footprinting
description: Run time-course ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag for JUN/FOS family members and H3K27ac before, during, and long after stimulus withdrawal. Test whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers opened by the stimulus stay accessible and bound once AP-1 activity has returned to baseline. This separates a memory-like chromatin state from continued AP-1 occupancy.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during maintenance versus establishment
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only during the rest period before re-challenge. Measure memory genes by accessibility and nascent transcription. If AP-1 is needed for establishing but not maintaining memory, it acts as an initiator. If it is needed for both, it is a maintenance mechanism.

title: Single-cell multiome and live-cell reporters of memory heritability
description: Pair single-cell RNA and ATAC profiling with live imaging of AP-1 activity reporters or endogenous tagged JUN/FOS. Track lineages through divisions to test whether memory states are heritable and bistable, and whether they correlate with AP-1 level, dynamics, or a positive feedback loop. Model the results to look for hysteresis.

title: Targeted synthetic perturbation of AP-1 sites at memory loci
description: Use CRISPR base editing or deletion of AP-1 motifs, together with dCas9-based recruitment or blocking of AP-1 at specific enhancers. Test whether memory at a given gene needs local AP-1 binding, and whether forced AP-1 occupancy alone is enough to create memory without a prior stimulus. Add measurements of nucleosome remodeling (BAF recruitment) and histone marks to define the mechanism.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury signal), let AP-1 activity return to baseline, then re-stimulate days to weeks later. Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, nascent RNA) and kinetics against naive cells to test for primed or enhanced responses.

title: Time-resolved chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy
description: Run ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag/ChIP-seq for FOS/JUN family members, and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 profiling before, during, and long after stimulation. Test whether AP-1-dependent enhancers remain open or poised after AP-1 binding disappears, indicating a persistent epigenetic trace.

title: Acute AP-1 perturbation to test necessity and sufficiency
description: Remove AP-1 at different times using dominant-negative FOS (A-FOS), degron-tagged JUN/FOS, or CRISPRi/KO, and pulse it with optogenetic or inducible expression. Determine whether AP-1 is needed only to establish the memory or also to maintain it, and whether a pulse alone is sufficient to create it.

title: Live imaging and single-cell multiome tracking of lineages
description: Use live reporters of AP-1 activity (e.g., FOS-GFP or AP-1 response element reporters) with lineage tracing, plus single-cell multiome (RNA+ATAC) over time. Quantify whether the memory persists through cell divisions, how heterogeneous it is, and whether prior AP-1 dynamics (amplitude, duration, pulsing) predict later responses.

title: Locus-specific causal editing of AP-1 motifs and chromatin state
description: Mutate or delete AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or recruit dCas9 effectors (writers/erasers of H3K27ac or DNA methylation) to them. Measure whether the primed state, and the enhanced re-response of nearby genes, depends on those sites and on partner pioneer factors or chromatin remodelers, such as SWI/SNF.

title: Prime-rest-restimulate time course with chromatin profiling
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a transient stimulus (TPA, TNF, or wounding cues), let them rest for days to weeks, then restimulate. Measure ATAC-seq, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN, and RNA-seq to see whether primed cells show faster or stronger transcription and retained accessibility at AP-1 motif sites compared with naive cells.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different memory phases
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS, JUN, or ATF family members and deplete them (a) during priming only, (b) during the rest period, or (c) during restimulation. Determine which window is needed to establish versus maintain the primed response, separating AP-1 as an initiator of memory from AP-1 as a continuous maintainer.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage-tracked memory
description: Combine single-cell ATAC and RNA with barcoded lineage tracing, so sister cells can be compared after priming. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target-gene expression states are inherited across divisions and heterogeneous among clones, consistent with heritable cell-state memory.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporters and dynamics imaging
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or AP-1 transcriptional reporters with single-molecule tracking and optogenetic or pulsed stimulation. Quantify whether past stimulus history alters the amplitude, duration, or dimer composition of later AP-1 responses, and whether this predicts the memory state of single cells.

title: Locus-specific causal perturbation of AP-1 sites
description: Use CRISPR base editing or dCas9 perturbation to mutate or block AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, and measure pioneer-like opening (with or without SWI/SNF/BAF inhibition) and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1). Test whether the motifs are necessary and sufficient for stable accessibility and enhanced re-induction after a transient signal.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Give cells a brief pulse of a stimulus that activates AP-1 (e.g., TPA, a growth factor, or an inflammatory cue), then run time-resolved ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) for days to weeks after signal removal. Memory would predict that a subset of AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stays open or marked after AP-1 returns to baseline.

title: Re-stimulation assays with transcriptional readouts
description: Compare primed and naive cells by RNA-seq or single-cell RNA-seq after a second stimulus given at varying intervals. Look for faster, stronger, or qualitatively different induction of AP-1 target genes in primed cells. The decay kinetics of this priming effect quantify how long the memory lasts.

title: Acute AP-1 loss-of-function during the memory phase
description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or dominant-negative A-FOS, and time the depletion to different phases: during the initial stimulus, or only after it has ended. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, depleting it later should leave accessibility and primed responses intact. If it is needed to maintain memory, they should be lost. Pair this with ATAC-seq and re-stimulation readouts.

title: Optogenetic or synthetic AP-1 activation to test sufficiency
description: Use a light- or drug-inducible FOS/JUN to give pulses of defined amplitude, duration, and dynamics in cells with no prior history. Measure whether the pulses alone cause lasting enhancer opening and stable target-gene priming. Then mutate the AP-1 motifs at selected loci with CRISPR, or use dCas9 effectors, to test whether the memory depends on those specific sites.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Perform single-cell multiome (RNA plus ATAC) on cells that have undergone several divisions after the stimulus, with clones tagged by barcodes. Test whether sister cells share accessibility states and primed responses and whether memory persists in a heritable, clone-specific way. Use live AP-1 activity reporters to determine whether memory is carried by AP-1 self-reinforcing loops (e.g., FOS/JUN autoregulation) or by chromatin states that persist without AP-1.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed chromatin accessibility readout
description: Expose cells to a defined pulse of AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then wash out and profile ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and H3K27ac at days to weeks later. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif sites after Fos/Jun levels return to baseline would indicate a memory-like state.

title: Acute degron depletion of AP-1 during the maintenance phase
description: After the initiating stimulus has ended, use an inducible degron (dTAG/AID) on JUN/FOS or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) to remove AP-1. If primed enhancers close and the enhanced secondary response is lost only when AP-1 is removed during the maintenance window, AP-1 is required for maintaining memory, not just establishing it.

title: Secondary-stimulus response assay (priming test)
description: Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, single-cell) of naive versus previously stimulated cells upon restimulation, with and without AP-1 perturbation at the priming stage. Faster or stronger induction of AP-1 target genes in primed cells, dependent on AP-1 binding at those loci, directly tests memory function.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporter and lineage tracking across divisions
description: Image single-cell AP-1 activity (e.g., FOS-GFP knock-in or AP-1 transcriptional reporter) with lineage tracing through cell divisions after a pulse stimulus. Heritable reporter states in daughter cells, and their dependence on feedback loops, would show whether memory is cell-autonomous and mitotically propagated.

title: AP-1 pioneer function and mitotic bookmarking tests
description: Perform CUT&RUN/ChIP on mitotic-arrested versus interphase cells and use motif-mutant (CRISPR-edited) enhancers or dCas9-based AP-1 site recruitment/blocking to ask whether AP-1 retention at specific sites is necessary and sufficient to reopen chromatin and sustain gene expression after division. Pair with ordering of AP-1 relative to SWI/SNF (BAF) recruitment and histone marks to define the mechanism.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a brief, defined stimulus (e.g., TNF, EGF, or PMA pulse), wash out, then re-stimulate after hours to days. Compare the magnitude and kinetics of AP-1 target gene responses (RNA-seq, nascent transcription by PRO-seq) with those of naive cells to quantify primed or memory-like responses.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy
description: Run ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for FOS, JUN and H3K27ac at time points before, during and long after stimulus withdrawal. Identify enhancers that stay open or acetylated after AP-1 levels return to baseline, and test whether motif-containing sites carry the persistent changes.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or after memory has formed. If memory requires AP-1 only at establishment, the epigenetic state persists after removal. If memory requires AP-1 at maintenance, it decays.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and heritability
description: Track AP-1 reporters, or endogenous FOS/JUN tagged with fluorescent proteins, in single cells over multiple divisions. Test whether activity states are inherited by daughter cells and whether the state depends on the history of past pulses, using lineage-resolved analysis and mathematical modeling of bistability or hysteresis.

title: Targeted perturbation of specific AP-1 sites
description: Use CRISPR to delete or mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers. Use dCas9-based activation or repression to impose or erase accessibility at the same sites. Then measure whether the primed response and chromatin state follow the edit, which tests causality at individual loci.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a defined stimulus such as TPA, TNF, or wounding. After a washout of days to weeks, re-challenge them and compare transcriptional kinetics and amplitude with naive cells by RNA-seq. A faster or stronger response that depends on AP-1 would indicate memory.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy
description: Profile chromatin accessibility, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) before stimulation, after it, and after a long washout. Identify AP-1 motif-enriched regions that stay open or primed once the signal is gone, and check whether those regions respond more strongly on re-challenge.

title: Acute AP-1 perturbation at different time windows
description: Use inducible dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS), degron-tagged JUN/FOS, or CRISPRi to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only during the memory (washout) phase. If memory requires AP-1 only for establishment, or also for maintenance, the effects on later responses and on accessibility will differ. This separates a role in establishing memory from a role in maintaining it.

title: Single-cell multiome and live-cell reporters of AP-1 history
description: Pair scRNA/scATAC multiome with live imaging of AP-1 activity reporters or FOS-GFP knock-ins to track individual cells and their lineages. Test whether a cell's past AP-1 activity predicts its later accessibility and responsiveness, and whether this persists through cell divisions, which would show heritable memory beyond a population average.

title: Targeted motif and site-specific causal editing
description: Mutate or delete specific AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers with CRISPR base editing, or block them with dCas9. Alternatively, use a massively parallel reporter assay or an integrated reporter to test whether enhancer priming and the memory response depend on those motifs. This tests whether the effect is local and sequence-specific, and whether it requires cofactors such as BAF/SWI-SNF, tested by inhibiting them.

title: Transient stimulus with AP-1 degron, then re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, wounding, or growth factor pulse), then acutely deplete AP-1 (FOS/JUN family) with a degron at different times after the stimulus. Re-challenge weeks later and measure whether the primed transcriptional response persists without AP-1 present, separating AP-1 as a maintainer from AP-1 as an initiator.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy and accessibility
description: Profile chromatin accessibility, AP-1 motif footprints, JUN/FOS binding, and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 at time points from during the stimulus to many cell divisions after its removal. Test whether AP-1-bound enhancers stay open or become 'latent' after the stimulus, and whether AP-1 binding is required to keep them so.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Combine single-cell RNA/ATAC with clonal barcodes or live-cell reporters to compare memory states in sister cells and across divisions. If AP-1-dependent states are heritable, sister cells should show correlated accessibility and re-activation kinetics beyond what is expected from shared environment.

title: Locus-specific perturbation with dCas9 tools
description: Use dCas9-based recruitment or blocking of AP-1 motifs, plus CRISPR deletion or mutation of specific motifs at candidate memory enhancers. Test whether altering a single AP-1 site abolishes or creates memory at that gene (faster re-induction, retained accessibility) in cis, independent of global AP-1 levels.

title: Dose, duration, and composition sweeps with live reporters and modeling
description: Vary the strength, duration, and frequency of stimuli and AP-1 dimer composition (e.g., FOS vs. JUNB vs. ATF3 overexpression) while tracking AP-1 activity and target gene reporters live. Fit mathematical models (hysteresis, bistability, positive feedback) to test whether AP-1 dynamics show the signatures of a self-sustaining memory circuit versus a purely transient signal-following response.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages, fibroblasts, or neurons) with a transient signal that induces AP-1, then run ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 (FOS/JUN), H3K27ac, and H3K4me1 at multiple time points after washout. Test whether AP-1-bound enhancers stay open and primed long after AP-1 activity returns to baseline, and whether a second stimulus gives a faster or stronger transcriptional response at those sites.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during memory maintenance
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 before priming, during the rest period, and at restimulation. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, accessibility should persist after removal; if it is needed to maintain memory, accessibility and the faster secondary response should decay.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of priming and response
description: Perform paired scRNA/scATAC-seq on naive, primed, and restimulated cells to link each cell's AP-1 motif accessibility to its secondary response. Test whether memory is heritable and graded (clonal, tracked with lineage barcodes across divisions) or an all-or-none state. Compare this against cells that were never primed.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporters, pulse history, and feedback dynamics
description: Use endogenous tagging of FOS/JUN and AP-1 transcriptional reporters, with optogenetic or pulsatile stimulation, to record single-cell dynamics over days. Test whether prior pulse history predicts later response amplitude or kinetics after AP-1 levels have returned to baseline, and whether the memory is carried by a self-sustaining feedback loop with bistable or hysteretic behavior.

title: Site-specific causal perturbation of AP-1 motifs
description: Use CRISPR editing of AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-based recruitment and blocking, at selected memory-associated enhancers. Then test whether priming-induced accessibility, histone marks, and faster re-induction of nearby genes are lost. Include perturbation of cooperation with SWI/SNF (BAF) and lineage factors such as PU.1 to distinguish AP-1 as the memory carrier from AP-1 as only one input to a broader chromatin state. Complement this with in vivo tests, for example in trained-immunity or injury-primed tissues after the stimulus is gone.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TNF, EGF, or PMA), let it wash out for hours to days, then re-stimulate and measure the transcriptional response (RNA-seq, nascent RNA) relative to naive cells. Compare the memory-linked response in wild-type cells and cells with AP-1 (FOS/JUN) knocked out or acutely degraded to see whether AP-1 is needed for the primed or altered response.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy profiling
description: Run ATAC-seq or scATAC-seq, plus CUT&RUN for JUN/FOS, before, during, and after stimulation and after long washout. Look for enhancers that stay open and keep AP-1 motifs or binding after the signal is gone, and test whether these sites carry H3K27ac or H3K4me1 and predict enhanced re-induction of nearby genes.

title: Acute degron perturbation at defined time windows
description: Use dTAG or auxin-inducible degradation of AP-1 components during the initial stimulus, during the memory (washout) phase, or during re-challenge. This separates AP-1's role in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it and from its role in executing the recall response.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and heritability
description: Track endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and AP-1 reporters in single cells through stimulation, washout, division, and re-stimulation. Quantify whether pulse history, level, or duration is retained and passed to daughter cells, and whether it predicts later reporter output beyond cell-to-cell noise.

title: Targeted enhancer editing and synthetic AP-1 recruitment
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers with CRISPR, and in separate experiments recruit AP-1 or its cofactors with dCas9 fusions at those sites. Test whether motif loss abolishes memory and whether forced AP-1 binding is sufficient to create a lasting accessible, primed state. Add perturbation of chromatin partners such as BAF/SWI-SNF to probe mechanism.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury), let signaling return to baseline, then re-stimulate days to weeks later. Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility against naive cells to test whether prior exposure leaves a lasting, AP-1-dependent change in response.

title: Time-resolved ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy and motif accessibility
description: Track chromatin accessibility, H3K27ac, and JUN/FOS binding at AP-1 motif-containing enhancers before, during, and long after the stimulus. Persistent opening or retained binding after AP-1 activity decays would indicate an epigenetic memory, and chromVAR motif analysis can quantify it.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion during memory maintenance phase
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 factors to remove AP-1 either only during the initial stimulus or only during the maintenance/recall phase. This separates AP-1 as the initiator of memory from AP-1 as the maintainer, and shows whether enhancer accessibility and primed responses persist without it.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory states
description: Perform single-cell RNA plus ATAC on stimulated and naive populations over time, combined with heritable barcodes or live reporters of AP-1 activity. This tests whether memory is carried by cell-autonomous states inherited through divisions, and whether it correlates with prior AP-1 dynamics in individual cells.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 activation to test sufficiency
description: Drive AP-1 factors (e.g., FOS/JUN) with light-inducible or pulsed expression at varied dose, duration, and frequency, then measure persistence of target gene expression and chromatin changes. Testing whether AP-1 alone is sufficient to create a lasting state, and how pulse patterns affect it, tests its causal role and tunability as a memory mechanism.

title: Stimulus-then-washout chromatin accessibility time course
description: Expose cells to a transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then track ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN, and H3K27ac at multiple timepoints after washout. Persistent accessible regions containing AP-1 motifs after AP-1 protein levels return to baseline indicate a memory-like chromatin state.

title: Re-stimulation response assay (primed vs naive)
description: Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) of previously stimulated versus naive cells upon a second challenge days to weeks later. Faster or stronger induction of AP-1 target genes in primed cells, with kinetics quantified, tests functional memory.

title: Acute AP-1 perturbation with degron or dominant-negative
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degradation or dominant-negative A-FOS during different windows (during priming, during the memory interval, or at re-challenge). Loss of memory only when AP-1 is removed during specific windows distinguishes AP-1 as the establishing versus maintaining mechanism.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage-tracing of memory persistence
description: Perform paired scRNA/scATAC-seq on primed cells and track clones through division with barcoding or live reporters. This reveals whether AP-1 accessibility states are heritable across cell divisions and how heterogeneous memory is among individual cells.

title: Synthetic sufficiency test with optogenetic or CRISPR-targeted AP-1 sites
description: Pulse AP-1 activity with optogenetic FOS/JUN, or use dCas9-based recruitment or deletion of specific AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers. Then measure whether accessibility, pioneer-factor cooperation (e.g., with BAF), and gene responsiveness persist after the pulse, testing sufficiency and locus-specific necessity.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TNF, wounding cues, or EGF), then perform ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and H3K27ac at multiple time points after withdrawal, including weeks later. AP-1 motif-containing open regions that outlast the stimulus and are absent in naive cells would indicate an epigenetic memory footprint.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to test necessity for maintenance
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/auxin) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming or only after the stimulus has ended. Then measure whether memory accessibility and faster or stronger transcriptional re-induction on restimulation are lost.
