description: Use dCas9 or a synthetic AP-1 (a tethered or optogenetic JUN/FOS) to bring AP-1 to a chosen locus for a limited time, and then test whether the locus keeps its accessibility and expression after the tool is removed. Compare wild-type motifs with motif mutants and with pioneer or SWI/SNF (BAF) recruitment-deficient variants, to test sufficiency and mechanism of AP-1-dependent memory.

title: Permanent labeling of cells with past AP-1 activity and re-challenge
description: Use a FOS/JUN knock-in fluorescent or recombinase-based reporter (e.g., Fos-CreER-style tagging) to permanently mark cells that experienced a stimulus, then follow marked and unmarked cells through divisions. Re-challenge and compare transcriptional response and chromatin state between marked and unmarked sister lineages to test whether past AP-1 activity predicts altered future responses.

title: Paired-stimulus priming with washout time course
description: Expose cells to a first AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or wounding), wash out, and re-stimulate after variable delays (hours to many cell divisions). Measure second-response magnitude by RNA-seq and nascent transcription, and test whether AP-1 dose, delay, and motif-linked gene sets quantitatively predict memory duration, using JUN/FOS dominant-negative (A-FOS) to test necessity.

title: Single-cell multiome of AP-1 motif accessibility persistence
description: Run scATAC+RNA-seq before, during, and long after stimulation. Track whether AP-1-motif (chromVAR) accessible regions stay open after AP-1 protein levels return to baseline, and whether heterogeneity in cell states (e.g., fast vs. slow) maps onto subsequent responsiveness at the single-cell level.

title: Acute degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Tag endogenous AP-1 factors (JUN, FOSL, BATF) with a degron and deplete them either during the priming stimulus or only after the memory state has formed. If memory sites (ChIP/CUT&RUN, ATAC, H3K27ac) persist and the enhanced response remains after AP-1 loss at later times, AP-1 is only an initiator; if memory decays, AP-1 is required for maintenance.

title: Synthetic AP-1 enhancer perturbation and live reporting
description: Use CRISPR dCas9 tools to edit or mutate specific AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers (CRISPRi or base editing), while using live-cell imaging of a reporter at the locus. Test whether the motif is causally needed for faster or stronger reactivation after a prior stimulus, and whether ectopic AP-1 motifs can install memory at a naive locus.

title: Time course of accessibility after transient stimulus and washout
description: Give cells a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA or a cytokine), wash it out, and run ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at several times from hours to weeks. This tests whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after the signal is gone and AP-1 levels have fallen.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Use a dTAG or auxin-inducible degron on JUN/FOS, or a dominant-negative A-FOS, applied either during stimulation or after it. If accessibility and transcriptional priming persist when AP-1 is removed after memory is set, AP-1 is an initiator but not a maintainer. If they are lost, AP-1 is needed continuously.

title: Secondary-challenge assay with single-cell multiomics
description: Give a primary stimulus, rest the cells, then give a second stimulus. Use scRNA-seq plus scATAC-seq to compare the faster or stronger gene induction in primed cells against naive cells. Link this to AP-1 motif accessibility and binding at the same loci, and test causality with AP-1 site mutations or CRISPRi at selected enhancers.

title: Live-cell AP-1 dynamics and lineage tracking
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a reporter of AP-1 target activity in single cells across divisions, following lineages after a pulse. Measure how long the state is inherited and whether it is heritable through mitosis, with mitotic bookmarking assessed by imaging and mitotic-chromosome ChIP, to determine whether the state is passed to daughter cells.

title: Synthetic enhancer-memory reporter and sufficiency test
description: Insert AP-1-motif-only synthetic enhancers driving a reporter into a neutral locus, with motif variants that differ in number, spacing and affinity. Pulse the cells, then measure persistence of reporter activity, accessibility and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at the locus. This tests whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to make a self-sustaining state, and whether it needs cooperating factors or positive feedback loops. Adding an AP-1 recruitment-only control separates binding from a pioneer-like chromatin-remodelling function (BAF recruitment).

title: Decay-kinetics time course of AP-1 chromatin accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Apply a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then run ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN and motif accessibility (chromVAR) at hours, days, and weeks after washout to test whether the early AP-1 state persists or decays. Persistent AP-1-dependent open sites after signal removal, with measured half-lives, would indicate memory rather than a transient response.

title: Primed vs. naive re-stimulation challenge with acute AP-1 degradation
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then restimulate and compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) to naive cells; repeat with a degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) of FOS/JUN applied only during priming versus only during recall. If AP-1 is needed at priming to produce faster/stronger recall but not at recall, it acts as a memory-writing factor.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of heritable AP-1 accessibility
description: Use paired scRNA/scATAC with barcoded lineage tracing to follow clones after a transient stimulus and test whether AP-1 motif accessibility is heritably maintained in daughter cells or reverts to baseline. Clonal correlation of AP-1 state across divisions, compared with random divergence between sister cells, quantifies heritability.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporter imaging of dynamics and bistability
description: Engineer knock-in FOS/JUN fluorescent reporters or AP-1 activity reporters and track single cells with time-lapse microscopy through pulse-and-washout protocols with varied pulse durations and doses. Hysteresis, bimodality, or sustained activity after the stimulus ends suggests a self-sustaining feedback memory; rapid return to baseline suggests none.

title: Ordering of AP-1 binding and epigenetic marks with synthetic recruitment
description: At AP-1-dependent loci, map H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and DNA methylation over time after stimulus, and use CRISPR motif mutation or transient dCas9-based forced AP-1 recruitment to test whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient to establish enhancer marks that outlast its presence. Marks that persist after AP-1 removal would indicate AP-1 initiates memory that is passed to chromatin, whereas persistent AP-1 occupancy itself would indicate AP-1 is the maintained state.

title: Paired-daughter lineage tracking of AP-1 state
description: Live-image AP-1 reporters (e.g., FOS/JUN endogenous tags plus a TRE-driven reporter) in single cells after a transient stimulus, then compare sister cells across several divisions. High sister-sister correlation that exceeds that of unrelated cells and persists after the stimulus ends would indicate heritable memory rather than ongoing signaling.

title: Transient pulse followed by time course of chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy
description: Give a defined stimulus pulse (e.g., TPA or a cytokine), wash it out, and run ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for JUN/FOS and H3K27ac over days to weeks. AP-1 motif-enriched sites that stay accessible after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate AP-1 left a lasting epigenetic change.

title: Acute degron depletion at different times after priming
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-degradable AP-1 subunit (e.g., c-JUN or FOSL1) and remove it either during priming or after it, then restimulate and measure the transcriptional response by RNA-seq. If depletion after priming still leaves the enhanced response, AP-1 is only needed to establish memory. If depletion abolishes the response, AP-1 is needed to maintain it.

title: Single-cell multiome of primed vs naive populations
description: Run joint scRNA/scATAC on primed, naive and re-stimulated cells, then infer motif activity with tools like chromVAR and SCENIC. Compare the faster or stronger gene induction at AP-1-dependent loci in primed cells, and test whether the primed subpopulation is a discrete, stable state.

title: Synthetic AP-1 sufficiency and necessity test with dCas9 and mutated motifs
description: Delete or mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers by CRISPR, and in parallel tether AP-1 or a pioneer-capable domain to naive loci using dCas9. Loss of memory after motif deletion, and induction of persistent accessibility and heightened response by tethering, would show necessity and sufficiency at specific loci.

title: Persistent AP-1 chromatin occupancy after a transient stimulus
description: Pulse cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) with a stimulus such as TNF, PMA or wounding, then wash out and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding by CUT&RUN and chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq at days 0, 1, 7 and 21. Memory would be indicated by accessible AP-1 motif sites that are retained after the stimulus has ended and the FOS/JUN transcripts have decayed.

title: Acute degron depletion to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use auxin-inducible degradation of FOS or JUN (or dominant-negative A-FOS) before, during, or after the priming stimulus. If AP-1 is needed only during priming but memory persists, it initiates memory. If depleting it after priming erases accessibility and the faster secondary response, it maintains memory.

title: Primed-versus-naive re-stimulation response with motif-site mutagenesis
description: Measure the transcriptional response (nascent RNA, PRO-seq) to a second stimulus in primed and naive cells, and identify the genes with enhanced responses. Then use CRISPR to mutate or dCas9-block the AP-1 motifs at selected enhancers to test whether those sites are necessary for the enhanced response. Add a reporter-based test of whether the primed state is cis-encoded.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and heritability across divisions
description: Track endogenous FOS/JUN with fluorescent knock-in tags and AP-1 reporters in single cells over time, with lineage tracing after a stimulus. Test whether the state is inherited by daughter cells and decays over a characteristic number of divisions, as expected for epigenetic memory, rather than reflecting continued signaling, and relate dynamics (pulsatile versus sustained) to the memory outcome.

title: Coupling of AP-1 to chromatin state, with in vivo test
description: Test whether AP-1 recruits BAF remodelers and deposits H3K27ac or H3K4me1 that persist, using BRG1 inhibition, ChIP/CUT&Tag and sequential perturbation. Then check in vivo, for example in skin or after inflammation, whether tissue cells retain AP-1-dependent accessible regions weeks after injury and respond faster on re-challenge.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 history
description: Live-image endogenous FOS/JUN with knock-in fluorescent reporters (and a stable lineage tracker) in single cells through a first stimulus, a rest period, and a second stimulus. Test whether prior activation history predicts the amplitude or kinetics of the second response.

title: Mapping AP-1-bound latent enhancers by ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN
description: Profile AP-1 binding (JUN/FOS CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility, and H3K27ac before, after, and long after stimulus withdrawal. Identify enhancers that stay open or primed after AP-1 levels return to baseline, and test whether they are the sites that drive faster or stronger reactivation.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Prime cells, then use degron-tagged (dTAG/auxin) JUN/FOS or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS to remove AP-1 at defined times: during priming only, during the rest period only, or at restimulation. Compare enhancer accessibility and transcriptional memory to distinguish AP-1 as the initiator of memory from AP-1 as its maintainer.

title: Dynamics-encoded memory via optogenetic pulse patterns
description: Drive AP-1 with optogenetic or chemogenetic input using varied pulse number, frequency and duration, then measure target gene output and chromatin state after a delay. Fit a model, such as a bistable or hysteresis model, to test whether AP-1 dynamics encode a persistent state that depends on input history.

title: Lineage inheritance across divisions with sister-cell and single-cell multiome
description: Track primed cells through mitosis with time-lapse imaging, or barcode them, then run paired scRNA/scATAC on sisters and distant relatives. Test whether the primed AP-1 target state is inherited, decays at a measurable rate, and is shared more by clonally related cells than by random cells, which would show cell-autonomous heritable memory rather than a persistent external signal.

title: Degradation of individual AP-1 subunits after priming
description: Acutely degrade individual AP-1 family members (FOS, FOSB, JUN, JUNB, ATF3) with dTAG/auxin degrons after a priming stimulus, and measure which are needed to maintain versus establish the primed response on restimulation. Irreversible loss of response after degradation versus recovery after degron washout distinguishes a maintained memory from a transient one.

title: Time course of chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy after priming
description: Prime cells (e.g., with cytokine, wounding signal, or growth factor), then profile accessibility and AP-1 binding (ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN) days to weeks after stimulus removal to test whether AP-1-dependent enhancers remain open once AP-1 levels have returned to baseline. Motif-footprint analysis and comparison with naive cells would show whether AP-1 sites are the persistent memory elements.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage-tracked clonal memory
description: Use barcoded clones and paired scRNA/scATAC to test whether primed AP-1 activity states and target gene responsiveness are inherited across cell divisions in sister cells more than in unrelated cells. Heritability estimates of AP-1 activity and faster re-induction of target genes indicate cell-intrinsic memory rather than persistent signalling.

title: Optogenetic/CRISPR perturbation of AP-1 sites with live reporters
description: Deliver defined pulses of light-controlled AP-1 activation (or dCas9 activation of FOS/JUN) while imaging an AP-1 reporter and endogenous target loci, varying pulse number, duration, and rest interval. A memory mechanism predicts a history-dependent, faster or stronger second response, and mutating specific AP-1 motifs in enhancers by CRISPR tests whether those sites carry the memory.

title: Pioneer-like function and causality of epigenetic marks
description: Measure H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and nucleosome remodeling (BAF recruitment) at AP-1 sites after priming, and test whether blocking BAF activity or deacetylation erases memory while forced retention of the marks preserves it. Combine this with an in vivo model (e.g., skin inflammatory memory) to test whether AP-1-dependent accessibility is necessary and sufficient for faster secondary responses.

title: Stimulus-order dependence of AP-1 dimer composition
description: Stimulate cells with ordered pulses (e.g., growth factor then stress, versus the reverse) and measure FOS/JUN/ATF family composition and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for each subunit). Test whether the same stimuli in different orders leave distinct, persistent AP-1 binding and transcriptional states.

title: Persistence of AP-1-bound sites after stimulus removal
description: Perform time-course ATAC-seq, H3K27ac and AP-1 CUT&Tag at days to weeks after a transient stimulus, tracking whether AP-1-bound enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 itself returns to baseline. Pair with acute degron depletion (dTAG) of FOS/JUN at different times to determine whether AP-1 is needed to maintain the memory or only to establish it.

title: Secondary-response test via AP-1 perturbation
description: Give primed and naive cells a second stimulus and compare faster or stronger induction of target genes (RNA-seq, nascent transcription). Use CRISPRi or mutation of specific AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers, plus dominant-negative A-FOS, to test if the enhanced second response requires those sites.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of AP-1 states
description: Use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with heritable barcodes or sister-cell pairs to test whether AP-1 activity states are inherited through cell division. Correlate sister-cell similarity in AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression versus random pairs to quantify heritability beyond shared environment.

title: Robustness of memory to perturbation
description: Challenge primed cells with competing signals, inhibitors of kinases (JNK/ERK) or chromatin writers, and paralog knockouts (e.g., FOSL1/FOSL2 compensation). Measure how robust the memory is and which AP-1 members, cofactors (BAF, p300) or feedback loops stabilize it, using live reporters of an AP-1 target for longitudinal readout.

title: Comparing decay rates of AP-1 memory components
description: Memory may persist in some layers (chromatin accessibility at AP-1 motifs) but decay quickly in others (FOS/JUN protein, phosphorylation). After a transient stimulus, measure FOS/JUN protein and mRNA, JUN phosphorylation, ATAC-seq accessibility at AP-1 motifs, and enhancer H3K27ac over time, and fit decay rates to determine which layer carries memory beyond AP-1 protein levels.

title: AP-1 priming of enhancers by prior stimulation
description: Apply sequential stimulation (primary then secondary challenge, with variable rest intervals) and use single-cell multiome (scATAC + scRNA) to test whether initial AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN/JUNB) opens enhancers that enable faster or larger transcriptional responses to the second stimulus. Also test whether this effect is lost when AP-1 is removed.

title: Acute degron removal after the priming stimulus
description: Use dTAG/auxin-degron alleles of FOS, JUN, or dominant-negative A-FOS induced either during priming, or only after priming during the rest period. If memory persists after AP-1 is degraded post-priming, AP-1 is only an initiator; if memory decays, AP-1 is needed for maintenance. Read out secondary response magnitude, chromatin accessibility and nascent RNA (PRO-seq).

title: Dose and duration dependence of memory (bistability)
description: Test for threshold behaviour by titrating stimulus strength and duration, using live-cell AP-1 reporters (FOS-GFP, AP-1 motif reporter) tracked over days in single cells. Look for a bimodal, hysteretic response in which cells above a threshold stay ON after stimulus removal and cells below it return to baseline. Model positive feedback (JUN autoregulation) mathematically to predict the threshold, then perturb to test it.

title: Locus-specific causal test by motif editing and dCas9 recruitment
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or recruit dCas9-FOS or dCas9-repressors. Then measure whether memory of that gene (faster re-induction, retained accessibility, inheritance across cell divisions and passages) is lost, or can be installed ectopically without a stimulus.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge (hysteresis test)
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a defined pulse of an AP-1-activating signal (TPA, TNF, or injury), wash out, then re-stimulate after days to weeks and measure the transcriptional response by RNA-seq and nascent-transcript assays. Memory predicts faster or stronger induction of specific genes than in naive cells, and the effect should be lost if c-Jun/c-Fos is knocked out (e.g., by degron) only during the first pulse.

title: Persistent chromatin accessibility and histone marks after AP-1 loss
description: Use ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN), H3K27ac and H3K4me1 before, immediately after, and long after stimulus to find enhancers that stay open or primed once AP-1 has left. Test causality by showing those enhancers are AP-1 motif-dependent via CRISPR motif mutation or dCas9 perturbation and that persistent accessibility predicts the enhanced re-response.

title: Single-cell tracking of AP-1 dynamics with live reporters
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN (or use a synthetic AP-1 reporter) and image single cells over days to determine whether memory is stored as sustained AP-1 activity, a self-sustaining feedback loop, or heritable chromatin marks after AP-1 returns to baseline. Correlating prior pulse history with later per-cell response and lineage inheritance across divisions separates cell-autonomous memory from population effects.

title: Acute degron-based necessity and sufficiency tests with timing control
description: Use inducible degradation of AP-1 (e.g., dTAG on JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS) during priming, during the memory interval, and during re-challenge. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, removal during the interval will have no effect, whereas an effect of removal then implies AP-1 is needed to maintain memory; also test sufficiency by transient ectopic AP-1 expression in naive cells.

title: Dose-dependence and decay kinetics of memory
description: Quantify how memory scales with pulse strength, duration, and number of repeats, and measure its half-life and persistence across cell divisions. Fit a dynamical model (e.g., bistable versus graded) and test its predictions, such as bistability with a threshold, by sorting cells and checking for bimodal, heritable states.

title: Sequential occupancy mapping of AP-1 co-binding
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, serum, or a stress signal), profile FOS/JUN family members, the pioneer partner, and chromatin accessibility (CUT&RUN/ATAC) over days to weeks. Test whether multiple AP-1 factors accumulate on the same enhancers and whether early binding of the lead factor predicts later accessibility and H3K27ac. Persistence of these sites after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate a memory-like state.

title: Acute degron depletion at defined times after stimulus
description: Use dTAG/AID degrons on c-Jun, c-Fos, or JunB to remove AP-1 either during the stimulus or after it has ended, then measure the primed transcriptional response to a second stimulus. If memory requires AP-1 only at induction, the enhancer state should persist after removal; if it requires AP-1 continuously, memory should collapse once AP-1 is removed. This distinguishes AP-1 as the inducer of memory from AP-1 as its continuing carrier.

title: Single-cell paired readout of AP-1 dynamics and re-stimulation response
description: Combine live-cell reporters for FOS/JUN activity (or a knock-in fluorescent tag) with a prime–rest–restimulate protocol, followed by single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC). Test whether each cell's AP-1 activity history, such as amplitude and duration, predicts its secondary response, and whether the memory is binary or graded across cells.

title: Enhancer-specific causal perturbation of AP-1 motifs
description: Use CRISPR base editing or saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, together with dCas9-KRAB or dCas9-based eviction, applied before or after priming. Measure whether the motif is required for establishing the open state, for maintaining it, and for faster re-induction of the linked gene. Compare with other motifs to show that the memory is attributable specifically to AP-1 sites.

title: Memory kinetics and heritability across cell divisions
description: Track primed chromatin state (accessibility, histone marks, nascent transcription by PRO-seq) in lineages after stimulus washout, using time-lapse lineage tracing or sorted daughter cells across multiple divisions. Fit decay models and test whether AP-1-dependent states are inherited through mitosis (mitotic-chromatin CUT&RUN for AP-1 bookmarking) or rebuilt each cycle, and compare half-lives with and without AP-1 perturbation to quantify AP-1's contribution to memory.

title: Trimmed-consensus scoring of AP-1 occupancy across independent assays
description: Profile AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and accessibility after a transient stimulus using several independent assays (CUT&RUN, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq with different antibodies, footprinting) and labs/replicates. For each locus, drop the extreme scores and average the rest, so that only sites with robust, reproducible persistence long after the stimulus is gone are called memory sites, not artifacts of one antibody or batch.

title: Separating priming potential from realized response
description: For each AP-1-bound enhancer, define a fixed baseline predictor (motif strength, prior accessibility, baseline binding) and a separate response measure (transcriptional output, e.g., nascent RNA/PRO-seq, upon re-stimulation). Model whether prior exposure increases the response beyond what the baseline predictor predicts, to test if AP-1 history adds information beyond sequence and chromatin state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after the stimulus ends
description: Test whether memory is established and maintained without ongoing AP-1. Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS added at defined times (during priming, after priming, before restimulation) and measure whether accessibility and faster re-induction are lost, to distinguish AP-1 as initiator versus maintainer of memory.

title: Motif mutation and dose titration at single enhancers to test threshold behavior
description: Use CRISPR base-editing of single AP-1 motifs (partial versus full disruption) and titrate stimulus dose and duration. Measure the effect on persistent accessibility and re-stimulation response to find threshold-like (nonlinear) behavior, which would indicate AP-1 sites act as discrete memory switches.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of memory inheritance through division
description: After transient stimulation, use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with lineage barcodes or sister-cell pairing, plus live imaging of AP-1 reporters or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN. Test whether primed AP-1 target states are inherited by daughter cells and correlate with AP-1 binding retained through mitosis (mitotic bookmarking), compared with unstimulated controls.

title: Single-cell ATAC/CUT&Tag of AP-1 motif accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., epithelial or immune cells with a wound/inflammatory cue), remove the stimulus, and track at single-cell resolution which AP-1 (FOS/JUN) motif-bearing enhancers stay open for days to weeks. Persistent accessibility at specific sites, heterogeneous between cells, would indicate stored state; compare to unstimulated cells and to cells re-challenged later.

title: Re-stimulation test of primed response with variable rest intervals
description: Give a first pulse of stimulus, rest for variable intervals, then a second pulse, and measure transcription (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) and AP-1 binding kinetics versus naive cells. Faster or stronger induction at AP-1-dependent genes that decays with rest time quantifies memory duration; variation of the response with pulse timing and dose maps the memory's dependence on stimulus history.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate establishment, maintenance, and recall
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 factors, depleting them before the first stimulus, during the rest period, or only at re-challenge. If depletion only at establishment erases memory while depletion during the rest period does not, AP-1 initiates but does not maintain it; loss with depletion at maintenance or recall shows AP-1 itself carries the memory.

title: Site-specific perturbation of AP-1 motifs at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or motif deletion at individual AP-1 sites, plus dCas9-based tethering of AP-1 or chromatin remodelers (e.g., BAF), to test whether single sites are necessary and sufficient for retained accessibility and faster re-induction. Rank sites by effect size to test whether a few key sites have disproportionately large effects on the larger accessibility pattern.

title: Live-cell imaging of AP-1 dynamics and lineage-tracked memory
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a target-gene reporter in single cells across stimulation, rest, and re-stimulation, tracking lineages through division. Correlating a mother cell's AP-1 history with its daughters' reporter responses tests heritability; single-cell traces may be noisy while population-level patterns resolve into distinct memory states.

title: Stimulus-washout chromatin accessibility time course
description: Expose cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts) to a transient stimulus such as TNF, LPS, or wounding cues, then wash out and profile ATAC-seq, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN and H3K27ac at multiple timepoints out to weeks. Persistent AP-1-motif-containing accessible sites after AP-1 binding itself has decayed would indicate a memory that outlasts the signal.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during induction versus maintenance
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 components to remove AP-1 either only during the initial stimulus or only after washout, then restimulate and measure the transcriptional response by RNA-seq and accessibility. If depletion during priming prevents memory but depletion during maintenance does not, AP-1 acts as an initiator; the converse implies it actively maintains the memory.

title: Combinatorial AP-1 motif grammar at memory-associated enhancers
description: Map memory-associated enhancers and quantify AP-1 motif number, spacing, orientation, and co-occurrence with partner TFs (e.g., ETS, CEBP, NFAT), using massively parallel reporter assays with systematically varied motif arrangements. Test whether specific rules of motif combination predict which sites retain memory and which return to baseline.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Combine single-cell RNA plus ATAC with barcode lineage tracing or sister-cell pairing after stimulation to test whether AP-1 activity states and accessibility are shared among sister cells across divisions more than expected by chance. High sister concordance that persists for generations and predicts the magnitude of the secondary response would support heritable memory rather than transient signaling.

title: Targeted epigenome editing of AP-1-dependent memory loci
description: Use dCas9-based tools (CRISPRi/KRAB) or base-editing motif mutation at individual AP-1-bound enhancers that stay open after stimulation, and test the effect on faster or stronger reinduction of the nearby gene. Locus-specific perturbation shows which sites are necessary and sufficient, and whether memory is cis-encoded or depends on global AP-1 levels.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing of AP-1 state
description: Barcode individual cells with unique heritable barcodes, give a transient AP-1 stimulus, and use single-cell RNA-seq with an AP-1 target signature to test whether sister cells share AP-1 activity states after washout more than unrelated cells do. Shared states across divisions would indicate heritable memory.

title: Scrambled-motif enhancer editing
description: Use CRISPR to scramble or delete AP-1 (TRE) motifs at candidate enhancers while leaving the surrounding sequence intact. Then test whether those enhancers lose primed accessibility and faster re-induction, which would show that the AP-1 motif itself is required for the memory.

title: Optogenetic pulse-history encoding
description: Drive AP-1 activity with optogenetic or chemogenetic control using different pulse patterns (single long, several short, and spaced pulses) that deliver the same total dose. Measure later target gene output to see whether the response depends on stimulus history and not only on current AP-1 level. History-dependent output is a functional signature of memory.

title: Time-resolved chromatin profiling after washout
description: After a transient stimulus, collect ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag data (FOS/JUN, H3K27ac) at several time points, from hours to multiple cell divisions. Identify sites that keep their accessibility or occupancy after AP-1 protein returns to baseline, and test whether the persistence predicts stronger re-induction of nearby genes.

title: Hysteresis and maintenance test by acute depletion
description: Ramp the stimulus dose up and then down and look for hysteresis, which indicates bistability. In parallel, use an inducible degron on AP-1 factors during the priming phase or only during the later memory phase. If depletion in the memory phase does not erase the primed response, AP-1 is needed for establishing but not maintaining memory; if it does erase the response, AP-1 is needed for maintenance.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge (hysteresis test)
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, growth factor, or stress) that activates AP-1 (Fos/Jun), let activity return to baseline, then re-stimulate after varying intervals and measure target gene transcription and AP-1 occupancy. Faster or stronger secondary responses that depend on the first exposure would indicate memory, as would a decay time constant longer than the half-lives of the Fos/Jun proteins. A response counts as memory only if it is reproducible and history-dependent rather than a one-off burst.

title: Chromatin accessibility and AP-1 footprinting over time
description: Run ATAC-seq or CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors, along with H3K27ac and H3K4me1, before, during and long after stimulation. Look for AP-1-dependent enhancers that stay open or primed after AP-1 levels have fallen, which would show the stimulus left a lasting chromatin mark. Motif-level footprinting across the time course can separate persistent occupancy from persistent accessibility.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 after the priming phase
description: Use a degron (dTAG/auxin) or a dominant-negative such as A-Fos to remove AP-1 either during priming or only after it, then test whether the primed state persists. If the memory survives AP-1 loss after priming, AP-1 acts as an initiator that sets epigenetic marks. If the memory is lost, AP-1 is needed continuously to maintain it. Comparing the two timings separates these two mechanisms.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and reporters
description: Track endogenously tagged c-Fos/c-Jun or an AP-1 reporter in single cells across repeated stimulations to test whether activity states are inherited through division. Compare sister-cell correlation and lineage trees against shuffled controls to determine whether response states are inherited, as expected for memory, or arise from independent noise.

title: Motif mutation and synthetic AP-1 site insertion to test necessity and sufficiency
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and separately insert a synthetic AP-1 site at a neutral locus, then measure whether transient AP-1 signalling produces lasting accessibility and primed transcription. Motif mutation tests necessity, and the synthetic insertion tests sufficiency for encoding the memory.

title: Shuffled null-model control for memory readout
description: Build a null model by shuffling AP-1 motif positions and ChIP/ATAC labels across the genome. Compare real persistence of AP-1 binding after stimulus withdrawal against this shuffled null to show that retained accessibility is not due to chance.

title: Stimulus-withdrawal time-course of AP-1 occupancy and accessibility
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a transient stimulus, remove it, and track CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN plus ATAC-seq at days 0 to 14. Sites that stay open and AP-1 bound long after FOS/JUN transcript levels return to baseline indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming vs. before
description: Use degron-tagged JUN/FOS (dTAG) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming or only during rechallenge. If memory persists when AP-1 is removed after priming, it is held by other factors. If it is lost, AP-1 maintains the memory.

title: Secondary stimulation response with motif mutation
description: Use CRISPR editing or dCas9 interference to mutate AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, then measure the enhanced transcriptional response to a second stimulus by RNA-seq or reporter assays. This tests whether specific sites are necessary for faster, stronger re-induction.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Perform paired scRNA/ATAC on clonally related sister cells after priming and several divisions. Test whether AP-1-linked accessibility is inherited more similarly within clones than across them, and whether it predicts each cell's rechallenge response.

title: Chromatin accessibility memory after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TPA, growth factor, or injury signal), then wash out and perform ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at time points over days to weeks. Persistent AP-1 motif-containing accessible sites after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate a retained memory state. Because the persistent sites are a sparse signal, they must be separated from noise by comparing against unstimulated controls and shuffled-motif backgrounds.

title: Acute degron depletion to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use auxin-inducible degron tagging of FOS or JUN (or a dominant-negative A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either during the stimulus or only after memory is established. If accessibility and the enhanced secondary response persist after depletion post-establishment, AP-1 is needed only for establishing the memory. If they collapse, AP-1 is needed for maintaining it.

title: Re-stimulation response assay (primed vs naive)
description: Give a first stimulus, rest the cells, then give a second stimulus. Compare RNA-seq and nascent transcription (PRO-seq) between primed and naive cells, and check whether the faster or stronger induction is limited to AP-1-bound loci. Include a no-first-stimulus control and a first-stimulus-with-AP-1-inhibition control to show the dependence.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Do single-cell RNA and ATAC profiling, with barcodes or live reporter imaging to identify sister cells, after a transient stimulus and several divisions. Test whether sister cells share AP-1 site accessibility and responsiveness more than random pairs, which would indicate mitotic inheritance. Live-cell AP-1 reporters can also show whether the memory is bistable or graded.

title: Sufficiency test by synthetic AP-1 perturbation and histone context
description: Use dCas9-based recruitment or an inducible pulse of AP-1 at a defined enhancer, and measure whether it creates lasting accessibility and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 after the trigger is removed. Pair this with perturbation of cofactors such as BAF/SWI-SNF, and with motif mutation by CRISPR base editing. This tests whether AP-1 alone is sufficient and which co-factors stabilize the memory.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed ATAC/CUT&Tag readout
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA or inflammatory cue) and then profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding by ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag after a long washout. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif sites after the signal and AP-1 activity have returned to baseline would indicate a memory-like chromatin state, which relies on site-specific marks being retained after the signal ends.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during priming versus washout
description: Use a dTAG/auxin degron on JUN/FOS, or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS, either during the priming stimulus or only during the washout, then test whether the enhanced re-response is lost. Loss when AP-1 is removed only during washout shows ongoing AP-1 is needed to maintain memory; loss only when removed during priming shows it acts as an initiator.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 reporter history
description: Image AP-1 activity with a live reporter or FOS/JUN biosensor across repeated stimulation pulses in single cells, then relate each cell's prior pulse history to its later response amplitude. Cell-to-cell heterogeneity and persistence of individual cells' response states over days and divisions would distinguish true memory from continued signaling.

title: Perturbing AP-1 sites at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs or tether dCas9-KRAB or dCas9-p300 at specific primed enhancers, and measure re-stimulation transcription (RNA-seq/PRO-seq) and H3K27ac. If memory-linked genes lose faster or stronger secondary responses only when their AP-1 motifs are disrupted, this shows AP-1 binding is causal rather than merely correlated.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and inheritance assay
description: Synchronize and sort primed cells, and map FOS/JUN occupancy on mitotic chromosomes by CUT&RUN. Follow lineage-tracked daughter cells through several divisions, measuring whether enhanced responsiveness and AP-1-associated accessibility are inherited. Retained AP-1 binding on mitotic chromatin and transmission of primed responses to daughter cells would support heritable memory.

title: Chromatin priming time course after a transient stimulus
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, serum, or injury) and use ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN over days to weeks to test whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after the stimulus is gone. Then apply a second challenge to test for faster or stronger transcription at those sites.

title: Combinatorial AP-1 dimer composition perturbation
description: Test whether AP-1 memory is encoded in which FOS/JUN/ATF dimers form, not just in total AP-1 activity. Use dimer-specific CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq plus targeted degradation of individual members (dTAG) to identify which dimer compositions at which enhancers are needed to maintain primed states.

title: Single-cell lineage-barcoded heterogeneity test
description: Label clonal lineages with unique barcodes, stimulate transiently, and use single-cell multiome (RNA plus ATAC) to test whether sister cells share AP-1 motif accessibility and response strength after division more than random cells do. Shared states would indicate heritable memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Prime cells, then remove AP-1 (inducible degron or dominant-negative A-FOS) after the stimulus ends and before re-challenge. If memory requires continuous AP-1, primed accessibility and the enhanced response should decay; if AP-1 only initiates memory, they should persist, which separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Synthetic AP-1 reporter with live imaging
description: Build a reporter containing AP-1 motifs in varied arrangements and spacings. Image single cells over multiple stimulus pulses with varied intervals to quantify hysteresis, pulse-history dependence, and decay time, and mutate motifs or add methylation inhibitors to test which sequence features and chromatin marks carry the memory.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed ATAC/CUT&RUN re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined stimulus (e.g., TPA or serum), wash out, and let AP-1 (FOS/JUN) levels return to baseline. Then map chromatin accessibility and AP-1 binding (ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN) days later and compare transcriptional responses to a second challenge with naive cells. The 'memory' should only become apparent when the second stimulus reveals the retained chromatin state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use a degron (dTAG/auxin) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus only, or only after washout. If primed accessibility and the faster re-response persist after AP-1 is gone, AP-1 acts as an initiator; if they are lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain the memory. Comparing the two outcomes separates the two roles.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of priming and heterogeneity
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC-seq across stimulus, washout and re-stimulation time points. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility in individual cells predicts the strength of the later response and whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells. Lineage barcoding or cell-division tracking would link inheritance to memory rather than to persistent signaling.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics and target loci
description: Image fluorescently tagged FOS/JUN together with a transcriptional reporter of an AP-1 target gene through repeated pulses. Quantify whether previous pulses change the amplitude, timing or probability of later responses, and whether this lasts across divisions. Fit the data with mathematical models of hysteresis or bistability to distinguish true memory (history-dependent, self-sustaining) from slow decay of the signal.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and histone-mark profiling at AP-1 sites
description: Profile H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and nucleosome remodeling (BAF/SWI-SNF) at AP-1-bound enhancers after the first stimulus and after washout. Then use dCas9-based editing to erase or install these marks, or mutate AP-1 motifs, at selected enhancers and test for causal gain or loss of primed re-responses, to link AP-1 binding to a persistent chromatin state at specific loci.

title: Heritable barcoding of stimulation history
description: Give cells a brief, distinct AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., anisomycin, TPA, or EGF) and record each cell's history with a heritable lineage barcode or fluorescent reporter. After a washout of days to weeks, test whether the original stimulus can be read out from chromatin accessibility (scATAC) and from the transcriptional response to a second challenge.

title: Priming and re-stimulation assay with ATAC-seq and AP-1 mapping
description: Stimulate cells once, wash out, rest them for several cell cycles, then re-stimulate. Compare the kinetics and magnitude of the second response with naive cells (RNA-seq, nascent RNA), map retained AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and accessibility at enhancers with ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN, and test whether sites that stay open predict which genes respond faster.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined times (dTAG/AID)
description: Use degron-tagged FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 at set times after the initial stimulus. Removal after the stimulus ends but before re-challenge tests whether AP-1 itself must persist to maintain memory, or whether it is only needed to establish it. Measure whether accessibility and the enhanced second response persist without AP-1.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and heritability
description: Image FOS/JUN reporters or endogenously tagged proteins in lineages over several divisions, using microfluidic pulse protocols that vary pulse number, duration and spacing. Quantify whether the dynamics of a mother cell predict those of its daughters, and whether second-response amplitude depends on the pattern of earlier pulses, which would suggest a history-dependent state rather than a transient one.

title: Pioneer-like activity and chromatin-mark causality tests
description: Test whether AP-1 recruits chromatin remodelers (BAF) and deposits H3K27ac or H3K4me1 at memory enhancers, and whether those marks persist after AP-1 is gone. Use dCas9-based epigenome editing to add or remove the marks at specific enhancers, or use an AP-1 motif mutation, and measure the effect on memory of the response. This separates AP-1 as the trigger that establishes the marks from the chromatin state as the carrier of memory.

title: AP-1 decay kinetics versus memory persistence with acute degron removal
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, wounding, or cytokine pulse), measure the half-lives of AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN/ChIP time course, live-cell FOS/JUN reporters) and of the chromatin accessibility it created (ATAC-seq). Then use acute degron removal (dTAG on FOS/JUN) at varied delays to test whether memory requires continuous AP-1 or persists after AP-1 is gone, and compare the rate of memory loss with the rate at which the re-stimulation response is lost.

title: Primed-response assay with single-cell multiome and lineage tracking
description: Give cells a first stimulus, let them return to baseline for days, then deliver a second stimulus and measure the primed response by scRNA+ATAC multiome, comparing naive, primed, and AP-1 dominant-negative (A-FOS) or degron-treated cells. Test whether the faster or stronger second response depends on AP-1 sites that stayed accessible after the first stimulus, and whether the dependence is cell-autonomous by tracking lineages via barcodes across division.

title: AP-1 dimer composition and partner factors as a code for stimulus history
description: AP-1 dimers (FOS/JUN/ATF/MAF families) combine with partner TFs (e.g., ETS, NFAT, lineage TFs) to produce composite motifs. Use paired perturbation of dimer composition and partner presence (CRISPRi/degron matrix) with ChIP/CUT&Tag and MPRA to test whether history is encoded in which dimer and partner pairs were engaged, a pattern neither input contains alone. Predict that a history-specific dimer/partner signature at enhancers can decode a cell's past stimulus from chromatin state with a classifier trained on known histories.

title: Weak-affinity AP-1 sites as memory elements
description: Use CRISPR base editing or saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 motifs at a memory-associated enhancer to create variants with weakened affinity, then test whether suboptimal sites are the ones that retain memory (e.g., sustained accessibility with slow decay), while consensus TRE sites respond quickly and lose memory. Quantify with MPRA and locus-specific live imaging (dCas9 or reporter) across stimulus histories, to test whether suboptimal motif affinity produces hysteresis.

title: Dose-history mapping of AP-1 responses to different stimulus types
description: Apply stimuli of different types (mechanical, inflammatory, growth factor, injury) with systematically varied intensity, duration, and spacing, and measure induced AP-1 composition, enhancer occupancy, and downstream gene state with time-resolved CUT&Tag and RNA-seq. Fit a dynamical (bistability/hysteresis) model to ask whether AP-1 responses show thresholds, history-dependent state transitions, and response-size distributions that differ by stimulus type even though the same factor is activated. Validate by predicting the outcome of untested stimulus sequences.

title: Persistence of AP-1 site occupancy despite turnover of individual AP-1 proteins
description: Test whether memory persists even though no single AP-1 protein or complex persists: use degron-tagged FOS/JUN family members, pulse-label with HaloTag, and run CUT&Tag at timepoints long after a stimulus. If sites stay occupied while the original molecules have turned over, memory is carried by exchanging subunits together with chromatin state. If occupancy requires the original molecules, it is not.

title: Single-cell accessibility record of sequential distinct stimuli at AP-1 sites
description: Stimulate cells with repeated, distinct pulses (e.g., TPA, then anisomycin, then serum) and run single-cell ATAC plus AP-1 motif-resolved footprinting. Test whether each stimulus leaves a separable, ordered accessibility signature at AP-1 sites that persists after washout and reflects stimulus history. Acutely removing FOS or JUN, or expressing a dominant-negative (A-FOS) after the stimulus, tests whether AP-1 is needed to maintain the signature rather than only to establish it.

title: Single-cell AP-1 fluctuation statistics as predictors of memory
description: Live-image an endogenous FOS/JUN reporter (MS2 or knock-in fluorescent tag) in single cells over days and measure the autocorrelation and pulse statistics of AP-1 activity. Test whether cells with higher pulse frequency or longer autocorrelation show a primed response (faster, stronger re-induction of target genes) on restimulation. Then use optogenetic control to deliver the same total dose as bursts or as a plateau, to test causally whether the temporal pattern encodes memory.

title: Perturbation of AP-1 sites to test sequence-encoded versus state-encoded memory
description: In cells with primed enhancers, use CRISPR to damage individual AP-1 motifs, or CRISPRi/dCas9 to transiently evict AP-1. Then quantify whether recovery leaves a stable epigenetic change, such as altered H3K27ac, DNA methylation, or reduced AP-1 re-binding, and whether the response to a second stimulus changes. Comparing wild-type, mutated-motif, and transient-eviction conditions separates sequence-encoded from state-encoded memory.

title: Test of AP-1 and a partner factor as a joint memory unit
description: Test whether AP-1 memory requires a partner such as a pioneer factor (e.g., ETS, CEBP, or SWI/SNF/BAF). Acutely degrade AP-1 or the partner after priming, and use sequential ChIP or CUT&RUN co-occupancy plus Micro-C to map the joint state. Memory lost only when both are present, or only when the partner is removed, would indicate that AP-1 recruits a memory-bearing complex rather than storing memory itself.

title: Tuning enhancer motif flanks, spacing, and affinity rather than knocking out AP-1
description: Instead of knocking out AP-1, use CRISPR base editing or dCas9 to subtly alter AP-1 motif flanking sequence, spacing, and affinity at primed enhancers. Then quantify how the strength and duration of the stimulus-induced memory response (ATAC accessibility, transcriptional re-induction kinetics) change. A graded dose-response of memory to motif affinity would show that AP-1 sequence encodes memory rather than merely being required for activation.

title: Footprinting of chromatin state after AP-1 loss
description: After transient stimulation (e.g., TPA, wounding signal, or inflammatory cue) and AP-1 washout, use CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors alongside ATAC footprinting, histone marks (H3K4me1, H3K27ac) and the SWI/SNF (BAF) complex to map accessible, BAF-marked sites that retain open chromatin once AP-1 is gone. Compare days to weeks later and with acute AP-1 degradation (dTAG/auxin degron) to test whether the memory persists independent of continued AP-1 binding or needs it to be maintained.

title: AP-1 memory across quiescence and division
description: Prime cells, then place them in quiescence (serum starvation or contact inhibition) or let them go through multiple cell cycles, for days to weeks without AP-1 activity (monitored with live AP-1 reporters). Re-challenge and test whether primed loci retain a faster, stronger response, and whether mitotic bookmarking by AP-1 (live-cell imaging, mitotic-chromosome ChIP) explains persistence, using degron removal of AP-1 during the dormant period as a causal control.

title: Single-cell lineage-traced memory with un-averaged readouts
description: Combine barcoded lineage tracing with single-cell multiome (scRNA + scATAC) to compare sister cells after a primary stimulus and re-stimulus, testing whether the response of one sister predicts the other's response beyond what shared AP-1 dynamics predict. Heritable, clone-specific, bimodal memory states that track with AP-1-dependent accessibility would be hidden in bulk averages and would distinguish true cellular memory from persistent signaling.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-pattern training
description: Use optogenetic control of AP-1 (e.g., light-inducible c-Fos/c-Jun or upstream kinases) to deliver defined pulse trains of varying frequency, duration and spacing, then measure whether later responses depend on the history of the pattern. Pair with live reporters of target genes and ATAC to build a map from stimulation history to cell state and test for hallmarks of memory: dependence on training pattern, spacing effects, decay time, and erasure by counter-stimuli.

title: Re-stimulation with and without injected noise to test hysteresis
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, wounding-related cytokines, or optogenetic FOS/JUN), then apply a second stimulus of varying strength and timing, with and without deliberately injected noise (pulsed or fluctuating dosing). Measure AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC) and target transcription; memory predicts a primed-versus-naive hysteresis loop in the dose-response, and the noise condition tests whether the memory state advances only under fluctuating input.

title: Persistence of AP-1-opened enhancer state after AP-1 loss
description: After priming, remove AP-1 with an acute degron on FOS/JUN, or a dominant-negative A-FOS, at several delays. Track by time-resolved ATAC, H3K27ac and H3K4me1 whether the accessible enhancer state persists and whether it accelerates re-induction of genes when AP-1 returns. If the state persists without AP-1 and drives faster re-induction, AP-1 acts as a writer of memory, not just a carrier.

title: Single-cell live reporters of AP-1 dynamics across divisions
description: Use live-cell reporters of endogenous FOS/JUN activity and a target gene in lineage-tracked single cells. Measure whether a mother cell's past AP-1 pulse history predicts response amplitude in daughter cells, and compute mutual information between history and response across generations. Cells that stay quiet in between serve as controls, since memory without ongoing AP-1 activity would indicate a carrier not bound by AP-1.

title: AP-1 binding-site editing and dCas9 tethering at primed enhancers
description: Mutate or CRISPRi/CRISPRa individual AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, and tether synthetic AP-1 or chromatin-remodeler recruiters at the same loci. Test whether a site is necessary and sufficient to confer faster, stronger secondary responses, which separates local enhancer memory from global cell-state memory.

title: Perturb-and-recover regulatory network reconstruction
description: Perform Perturb-seq or multiome sequencing at different times after a transient AP-1 stimulus, deleting AP-1 family members (FOS, JUN, ATF, MAF), and determine how the regulatory network (TF-to-enhancer-to-gene links) changes. Compare the rebuilt networks to the original and to naive cells and quantify path-dependence; stable differences after washout would indicate that AP-1 set a persistent network state.

title: Disruption and synthetic rescue of AP-1 motifs in stimulus-opened enhancers
description: Use CRISPR to disrupt individual AP-1 motifs in enhancers that gained accessibility after a transient stimulus (e.g., FOS/JUN induction or injury), then rescue them with synthetic motifs at shifted positions. Measure by ATAC-seq whether accessibility and H3K27ac persist at the disrupted or rescued site after the stimulus ends, and measure re-stimulation response magnitude weeks later.

title: Dose titration of AP-1 pulse dynamics and memory
description: Deliver defined AP-1 activation pulses (optogenetic FOS/JUN or c-Jun degron systems) varying in duration, amplitude and frequency, then wash out. Quantify retained accessibility and faster transcriptional re-induction on secondary challenge, to test whether memory requires a threshold of AP-1 dwell time rather than simple presence.

title: AP-1 occupancy decay versus chromatin persistence, with delayed degradation
description: After a stimulus, time-resolve AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for JUN/FOS) alongside accessibility, histone marks and nascent transcription over days to weeks and through cell divisions. If AP-1 leaves while accessibility persists, AP-1 acts as a pioneer factor that initiates the state. If its presence is required, acute degradation (dTAG) at various delays after the stimulus should erase memory only within a defined window, so the delay itself is the measurement.

title: Paired lineage-matched primed versus naive single-cell multiome comparison
description: Use single-cell multiome (ATAC+RNA) on matched primed and naive clones or lineage-barcoded sister cells, and rank-compare AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR) and target gene responsiveness only within pairs. Test whether sister-cell pairs inherit the same relative AP-1 state across divisions, giving a heritability estimate of the memory independent of batch or absolute signal.

title: Composite motifs of AP-1 with a second transcription factor at memory loci
description: Map composite motifs (AP-1 plus ETS, NFAT, or glucocorticoid receptor) genome-wide. Use MPRA and genomic perturbations to test whether memory loci are specifically those where AP-1 partners with a cell-type factor. Knock out each partner separately and together to test whether retained accessibility requires the combination.

title: Periodic AP-1 stimulation with varied schedule
description: Expose cells to AP-1-activating stimuli (e.g., TPA, anisomycin, optogenetic c-Fos/JUN) in periodic regimes with varied period and duty cycle, then measure chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target-gene response to a later test challenge. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, the priming should depend on the schedule (frequency tuning) and not just on total dose, and should outlast AP-1 protein levels.

title: Footprinting of AP-1 sites that stay accessible after stimulus withdrawal
description: After transient stimulation, track time-resolved ATAC/CUT&Tag with TF footprinting to find AP-1 motif sites that remain open after AP-1 occupancy is lost. Compare with H3K27ac/H3K4me1 and with sites in never-stimulated cells to test whether the accessible state persists and carries memory without ongoing AP-1 binding.

title: Acute degradation of FOS/JUN at defined stages
description: Use degron-tagged FOS or JUN (or dominant-negative A-FOS) to remove AP-1 before the priming stimulus (to test a role in establishing memory), during the resting interval (maintenance), and at re-stimulation (readout). Measure RNA-seq and accessibility on re-challenge to separate establishment, maintenance and recall roles.

title: Single-cell lineage tracking of AP-1 history with recorder reporters
description: Use a live AP-1 activity reporter, such as a destabilized and stable fluorescent reporter pair or a Cre-based recorder that permanently marks past AP-1 activation, combined with lineage tracing and later re-stimulation. Test whether cells and their daughters with a recorded AP-1 history respond more strongly or faster, and for how many divisions, to separate cell-autonomous heritable memory from ongoing signaling.

title: Mutating AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or enhancer-deletion screens (MPRA plus endogenous editing) to alter AP-1 motif number, spacing and affinity at loci that show primed responses. Measure how these changes shift the strength and duration of the memory phenotype, to test whether AP-1 sites are necessary and sufficient, and whether suboptimal motif quality tunes the rate of memory decay.

title: Mapping accessibility loss after AP-1 or BAF perturbation in previously stimulated cells
description: After a transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), perturb the cells with AP-1 degron depletion or BAF inhibition, and map which enhancers lose accessibility (ATAC/CUT&Tag) and in what order. Compare the pattern of accessibility loss between naive and previously stimulated cells to test whether it reflects the history of earlier AP-1 exposure.

title: Analysis of sites AP-1 binds but fails to open
description: Use time-resolved ChIP/CUT&RUN plus ATAC across repeated stimulations to catalog AP-1 motif sites that are bound transiently but never become accessible or never retain accessibility. Compare their sequence, nucleosome, and cofactor features with sites that are retained to define the rules for which AP-1 binding is converted into memory and which is not.

title: Two offset AP-1 stimulus rhythms and timing-dependent memory
description: Deliver optogenetic or chemical AP-1 pulses at two slightly offset periods or through two pathways (e.g., JNK and ERK), then measure whether residual enhancer accessibility and gene expression show a slow beat pattern or phase-dependent memory. The aim is to test whether AP-1 integrates stimulus timing rather than just dose, and to distinguish dynamics-based memory from a simple ratchet mechanism.

title: Graded, time-specific reduction of AP-1 dosage to find a memory threshold
description: Use titratable degrons (dTAG/AID), CRISPRi alleles of FOS/JUN family members, and motif-site edits to reduce AP-1 stepwise at defined times (during priming, during the delay, or during recall), instead of overexpressing it. Measure recall amplitude and chromatin state to separate AP-1's roles in establishing, maintaining, and reading out memory, and to identify any dose threshold.

title: Lineage-tracked inheritance of the primed state through division and passaging
description: Prime cells with an AP-1 stimulus, then serially passage them with strong dilution, using barcoded lineages, single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) and live AP-1 reporters. Test whether the primed state persists, is heritable by clone, and re-establishes after dilution without the stimulus, and whether passing it on requires continued AP-1 binding (acute degron versus no degron). Persistence through repeated dilution would indicate a self-propagating state.

title: Stimulus-order permutation with chromatin readout
description: Expose cells to many different orderings of the same pulses (e.g., TNF, EGF, stress, or phorbol ester), with each ordering differing from another by a change in only one adjacent step. Then measure ATAC-seq accessibility at AP-1 (FOS/JUN) motif sites and the transcriptional response to a common test challenge. If the response depends on order and not just total dose, AP-1 acts as a history-dependent memory.

title: Mapping persistently open enhancers after AP-1 departure
description: Use CUT&RUN or CUT&Tag for FOS, JUN, and H3K27ac, plus ATAC-seq, at several times after a transient stimulus to find enhancers that stay open after AP-1 has left. Test whether persistence of these sites predicts a stronger secondary response, and use acute degron removal of AP-1 (dTAG or AID) after priming to test whether maintenance requires continued AP-1 binding or only the initial engagement.

title: Live single-cell AP-1 reporter imaging with lineage tracking
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN, or an AP-1 transcriptional reporter, across cell divisions and re-stimulations, treating cell-to-cell variability as the signal. Test whether sister cells share activation states more than random pairs do, and for how many generations. Quantify memory using mutual information between past and future responses, and compare with a control in which AP-1 dynamics are optogenetically clamped.

title: Optogenetic or chemogenetic AP-1 induction with sufficiency tests
description: Drive JUN/FOS with a light- or drug-inducible system using pulse patterns that differ in duration, frequency, and dimer composition, then remove the input and track target gene expression, chromatin state, and responsiveness to later challenges. Whether a defined pulse pattern is sufficient to create a lasting, heritable state, and whether this depends on dimer identity, would test AP-1 as a causal writer of memory rather than a correlate.

title: Cofactor, feedback, and synthetic-locus dissection of memory maintenance
description: Test whether memory resides in AP-1 itself or in surrounding factors by combining CRISPRi or dominant-negative (A-FOS) perturbation of AP-1 with perturbation of cofactors and chromatin machinery (SWI/SNF, p300, histone methyltransferases) and of the FOS/JUN positive-autoregulatory loop. Measure memory half-life after each perturbation, and use mathematical modelling to distinguish bistable feedback from epigenetic-mark inheritance. Finally, insert AP-1 sites into a synthetic locus to test whether the motif alone can store state.

title: Chromatin accessibility memory readout after transient stimulus (ATAC/CUT&Tag)
description: Give cells a brief inflammatory or injury stimulus (e.g., TNF or wounding), wash it out, and profile AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and chromatin accessibility by CUT&Tag and ATAC-seq at days 0, 1, 7 and 28. Compare AP-1 motif sites in primed cells with those in naive cells to test whether they remain persistently open after stimulation.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during and after priming
description: Use a degron (dTAG/AID) on JUN or FOS, or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS, to deplete AP-1 either only during priming or only after the stimulus has been removed. If AP-1 is needed to establish but not maintain memory, the primed state should persist after depletion in the later window; if it is needed for maintenance, the state should decay. This separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Re-stimulation response test with single-cell multiome
description: Prime cells, rest them, then re-challenge. Measure faster or stronger induction of target genes with scRNA-seq plus scATAC, and link it to the AP-1 motif accessibility of individual cells. Naive cells are the control, and a non-AP-1 priming stimulus is a second control. A memory mechanism predicts a heterogeneous but heritable primed subpopulation whose response scales with its retained AP-1 sites.

title: Lineage-tracing of memory through cell division
description: Track daughter cells with live reporters (a fluorescent AP-1 activity reporter, or endogenous FOS/JUN knock-in tags) and barcoded lineages after a pulse stimulus. Test whether sister cells share the primed state for several divisions, and whether mitotic bookmarking by AP-1 on chromatin (imaged or by mitotic ChIP) explains it. Such inheritance would separate true memory from a lingering signal.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and mathematical modeling of bistability
description: Use dCas9 to open or close one AP-1-bound enhancer, and fit an ODE model of AP-1 feed-forward and positive-feedback loops with chromatin states. The model predicts hysteresis, meaning different response thresholds with increasing versus decreasing stimulus. Test this by dose-response titration of the stimulus, and check whether editing a single site shifts or abolishes the memory.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge (priming test)
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury signal), remove it, then re-stimulate after days to weeks and compare transcriptional responses to naive cells. Measure ATAC-seq, RNA-seq and FOS/JUN occupancy (CUT&RUN) to see whether AP-1-dependent primed or enhanced responses persist after AP-1 protein levels return to baseline.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degradation or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either only during priming or only after priming, before re-challenge. If memory persists after AP-1 removal, AP-1 is only the initiator. If it is lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain the memory. Readouts are chromatin accessibility and the secondary response.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of chromatin and expression states
description: Run paired scATAC/scRNA-seq at multiple times after stimulation and after resting. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility, AP-1 target expression and enhancer states are inherited by daughter cells, using lineage barcodes or sister-cell pairs to separate heritable memory from persistent signaling.

title: Enhancer-level epigenetic readout and engineered AP-1 sites
description: Map H3K27ac, H3K4me1, DNA methylation, and nucleosome remodeling (BAF) at AP-1-bound enhancers before, after, and long after stimulation. Then use dCas9 or motif mutation to delete or insert AP-1 sites at selected enhancers to test whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient to leave a persistent open, primed state.

title: Live-cell reporters and mathematical modeling of feedback
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a downstream reporter in single cells during pulses of different duration and frequency. Fit bistable or positive-feedback models and test predictions, such as hysteresis and a threshold dose, by perturbing feedback loops (e.g., JUN autoregulation) to see if AP-1 dynamics alone can store state.

title: Degron-based AP-1 depletion in haploid cells to test memory maintenance
description: Use haploid cells with an auto-inducible degron on FOS/JUN family members, and deplete AP-1 at defined times after a transient stimulus. Then measure by ATAC-seq whether the stimulus-induced chromatin accessibility and the faster transcriptional re-response persist without AP-1 (memory is AP-1-independent) or decay (AP-1 maintains it).

title: Prime–rest–restimulate time course with dose and interval series
description: Give a priming stimulus, wash it out, and re-challenge after varied intervals, measuring nascent RNA (PRO-seq) and target gene induction kinetics. If memory exists, primed cells should respond faster or more strongly, and the decay half-life of this effect can be compared between wild-type and AP-1-perturbed cells.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 reporters with lineage tracking
description: Track AP-1 activity with live reporters or a FOS-GFP knock-in across cell divisions and lineages. Test whether the active or primed state is inherited by daughter cells more than expected by chance, and whether it correlates with later responsiveness.

title: Pioneer-like binding and chromatin state profiling over time
description: Run CUT&RUN or ChIP for JUN/FOS and for H3K27ac and H3K4me1, together with ATAC-seq, before, during and after stimulation. Identify enhancers that stay AP-1 bound or open after the signal is gone, and test whether those sites are the ones that drive faster re-induction.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory-associated sites by CRISPR
description: Use dCas9 inhibition or activation, or motif mutagenesis, at persistently accessible AP-1 sites. Test necessity by asking whether editing the AP-1 motif abolishes the primed response at that locus, and sufficiency by asking whether forcing AP-1 binding in naive cells induces a primed state without a stimulus.

title: Accessibility memory after a transient stimulus and recall
description: Give cells a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA or a wound-like signal), wait until AP-1 (FOS/JUN) levels return to baseline, then re-stimulate and compare ATAC-seq, H3K27ac CUT&RUN, and transcription between naive and primed cells. Accessible sites that persist after the trigger is gone, with faster or stronger re-induction there, would indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different times (necessity for maintenance vs. establishment)
description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or a dominant-negative A-FOS, removed either during priming, during the rest period, or at re-stimulation. If memory needs AP-1 only during priming but not for later maintenance, AP-1 is an initiator. If memory is lost when AP-1 is removed during the rest period, AP-1 is a maintainer.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking with lineage barcodes
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC-seq with live reporters of AP-1 activity and heritable barcodes across divisions after a transient stimulus. Test whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells and whether it correlates with the AP-1 motif accessibility of a clone, separating a stable epigenetic state from ongoing signaling noise.

title: AP-1 pioneer-like binding and nucleosome remodeling kinetics (footprinting, BRG1/BAF dependence)
description: Measure AP-1 occupancy by CUT&RUN or footprinting, together with BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment and histone marks, at primed loci over a time course after the stimulus is withdrawn. Test whether AP-1 sites stay open after AP-1 departs (hysteresis) by inhibiting BAF, and whether a mutated motif at an endogenous enhancer (CRISPR base editing) abolishes the memory.

title: Synthetic sufficiency and dose-history test with optogenetic AP-1 and a mathematical model
description: Drive AP-1 with optogenetic pulses of defined amplitude, duration and spacing, and read out reporter or endogenous gene responses over the following days. Fit bistability and hysteresis models, and test whether activation of AP-1 alone is sufficient to create a persistent state at naive loci that depends on pulse history and not just on current AP-1 levels.

title: Pulse-chase profiling of AP-1 occupancy and accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells briefly (e.g., TPA or serum), remove the stimulus, and profile AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and chromatin accessibility by CUT&RUN and ATAC at defined time points over days. Sites that stay open after AP-1 binding has been lost, compared with unstimulated controls, would indicate AP-1-dependent memory.

title: Re-stimulation response with timed AP-1 degron
description: Give a priming stimulus, rest the cells, then re-stimulate and measure transcription (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) in primed versus naive cells. Use an acute degron (dTAG/auxin) on FOS/JUN either during priming only or during re-stimulation only, to distinguish a role for AP-1 in establishing memory from a role in reading it out.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracking of memory persistence
description: Run scRNA+scATAC with a barcoded lineage label to follow primed clones through several divisions. Test whether accessibility and gene-expression states at AP-1 motifs are inherited by daughter cells more than expected from shared environment, using sister-cell concordance and decay rates.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics and target gene state with modeling
description: Image a FOS/JUN fluorescent knock-in alongside MS2/PP7 or destabilised-reporter readouts of target loci during repeated pulses. Fit a quantitative model to see whether prior pulses change the amplitude, kinetics or bistability of later responses (hysteresis), which would be the signature of memory.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory sites and AP-1 motifs
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-based tools (KRAB or p300) at sites that stay open after priming, then test whether the primed response is lost and whether forcing the site open without AP-1 restores it. Pair this with ChIP or CUT&Tag for H3K27ac and with pioneer-factor cofactors (e.g., BAF/SWI-SNF) to identify the mechanism of persistence.

title: Stimulus-withdrawal chromatin accessibility time course (ATAC-seq + CUT&Tag)
description: Stimulate cells transiently (e.g., TNF, wounding, or an inflammatory signal), then remove the stimulus and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and ATAC accessibility at its target enhancers over days to weeks. Persistent accessibility or H3K27ac at AP-1 motifs after AP-1 binding has decayed would indicate AP-1-established memory, as in the epigenetic changes seen in inflamed epithelium.

title: Acute degron depletion at priming vs. recall stages
