description: Use dTAG/auxin degrons on FOS/JUN family members (or dominant-negative A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either during the first stimulus, during the rest interval, or only at re-stimulation. If depleting AP-1 only during priming abolishes the faster or stronger secondary transcriptional response, whereas depletion during rest has no effect, AP-1 is needed to establish memory but not to maintain it; the opposite pattern shows it actively maintains memory.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage/history barcoding
description: Perform paired scRNA/scATAC-seq on cells with and without prior stimulation, with a heritable barcode or fluorescent AP-1 reporter recording previous exposure. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR) and memory-gene expression stay correlated across cell divisions in clonal lineages, separating heritable (mitotically stable) memory from transient signaling noise.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporter with optogenetic pulse patterning
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or an AP-1 transcriptional reporter while delivering controlled optogenetic or ERK-pulse inputs of varying duration, frequency, and rest interval. Fit input-history-dependent response curves (hysteresis, paired-pulse enhancement) to determine whether the system integrates past dynamics and for how long, giving quantitative memory timescales.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory-associated AP-1 sites with chromatin conformation readout
description: After priming, use CRISPRi/dCas9 epigenome editing or motif mutation at selected AP-1-bound enhancers (identified by persistent accessibility), and combine with Hi-C/Micro-C to look for retained loops. Test whether disrupting the AP-1 site or its recruited BAF/SWI-SNF remodeling erases faster re-induction of linked genes, establishing sufficiency and necessity at specific loci rather than genome-wide correlation.

title: Chromatin accessibility memory after transient stimulus (ATAC-seq time course)
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TNF, wounding, or growth factor), then wash out and profile ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at days to weeks. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif sites after AP-1 binding has decayed would show that AP-1 opens chromatin and that the open state is retained.

title: Acute degron depletion to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use auxin-inducible degradation of c-JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS at defined windows: during the stimulus only, or only after the memory is established. If depleting AP-1 during induction abolishes the later enhanced response but depleting it afterward does not, AP-1 is needed to establish but not to maintain memory (and vice versa), which tests whether AP-1 itself stores the state.

title: Secondary-challenge assay with single-cell readout
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then re-stimulate and measure transcription of AP-1 target genes by scRNA-seq or live reporters, comparing to naive cells. Faster or stronger responses in primed cells, with and without AP-1 perturbation, quantify memory, and single-cell data reveal whether the state is graded or bistable and heritable across cell divisions.

title: Pioneer-like binding and histone mark dynamics at AP-1 sites
description: Track H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and BAF/SWI-SNF (BRG1) occupancy with CUT&Tag over time at primed AP-1 sites, and test with AP-1 motif mutation via CRISPR base editing or dCas9 interference at selected enhancers. Mark persistence that requires the motif and recruited remodelers would show a mechanistic route from transient AP-1 binding to a lasting epigenetic state.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 perturbation with ODE modeling of memory mechanisms
description: Control AP-1 activity with optogenetic or chemically induced pulses of varied duration and frequency, measure the resulting target gene state at later times, and fit ODE models of positive feedback (FOS/JUN autoregulation) versus chromatin-based memory. Model comparison, such as hysteresis and dependence on pulse number, discriminates network-based memory from epigenetic memory.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages, fibroblasts) with a transient signal, then profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at timepoints through weeks after washout. Memory is supported if AP-1-bound enhancers stay open and primed after stimulus clearance and give faster, stronger transcription upon restimulation.

title: Acute degron depletion of AP-1 during versus after priming
description: Use dTAG/auxin degrons on JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to deplete AP-1 either only during priming or only after priming (maintenance phase). If priming-phase loss abolishes the enhanced secondary response while maintenance-phase loss does not, AP-1 is needed for establishment but not maintenance; the reverse pattern would show AP-1 itself maintains the memory.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage/history tracing of AP-1 activity
description: Combine an AP-1 reporter or recorder (e.g., Cre-based or fluorescent timer under TRE elements) with scRNA/ATAC multiome to label cells that experienced AP-1 activity and follow them after rest. Test whether past AP-1 history predicts accessibility state and restimulation response in individual cells, separating cell-autonomous memory from population heterogeneity.

title: Synthetic AP-1 recruitment sufficiency test
description: Use a dCas9-based or optogenetic system to transiently recruit AP-1 factors (or their pioneer-like partners) to a defined locus with a reporter. Then remove the trigger and measure whether accessibility, histone marks (H3K27ac/H3K4me1), and responsiveness persist across cell divisions. Persistence sufficient to alter later induction would show AP-1 can initiate memory by itself.

title: Live-cell imaging and kinetic modeling of AP-1 dynamics and division inheritance
description: Track endogenously tagged FOS/JUN with single-molecule or live imaging, and measure binding residence time, nuclear levels, and mitotic bookmarking across divisions in mother-daughter pairs. Fit mathematical models (bistable feedback vs. chromatin-based epigenetic memory) to determine which explains retention and inheritance of responsiveness; AP-1 autoregulation (JUN induces JUN) is a candidate positive-feedback mechanism.

title: Priming assay with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TNF, EGF, or PMA), wash it out for hours to days, then re-stimulate and measure transcription of AP-1 target genes by RNA-seq and nascent RNA (PRO-seq). Compare naive, primed, and AP-1-depleted cells; a faster or stronger second response that is lost when AP-1 is inhibited would show an AP-1-dependent memory.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy tracking
description: Run ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN family members, and H3K27ac ChIP at time points before, during and long after the stimulus. Identify enhancers that stay open and AP-1-bound after the signal has gone. Motif footprinting would show whether AP-1 binding persists or whether only an epigenetic mark remains.

title: Acute degron perturbation at defined memory phases
description: Fuse AP-1 subunits (c-JUN, FOSL1, or a dominant-negative like A-FOS) to a degron or place them under inducible control. Remove AP-1 either only during the initial stimulus (testing establishment) or only after the stimulus ends (testing maintenance), then re-challenge the cells. This separates a role for AP-1 in establishing memory from a role in maintaining it, and controls for general cell responsiveness.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 reporters with lineage tracking and modeling
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or a fluorescent AP-1 transcriptional reporter in single cells across stimulation, rest, and re-stimulation, and follow daughter cells through divisions. Measure whether activity states persist, are heritable, and are bistable, using autocorrelation between mother and daughter cells. Fit the data to a mathematical model of positive feedback (JUN autoregulation) to test whether the memory is a cell-intrinsic state.

title: Targeted epigenome editing of AP-1 sites to test sufficiency and necessity
description: Use dCas9-based tools (KRAB or p300) or motif mutations through CRISPR base editing to alter specific AP-1-bound enhancers that stay accessible after the signal. Test whether closing them erases the primed response, and whether forced AP-1 binding or opening creates a memory without the stimulus. Readouts are the gene expression response to re-challenge and the persistence of chromatin marks, which would show causality at single loci.

title: Transient stimulus with long-delay re-challenge (primed response)
description: Expose cells to a brief AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or injury signal), let AP-1 activity return to baseline, then re-stimulate after days to weeks and measure transcriptional output by RNA-seq. A memory would show as a changed second response compared with naive cells, and the change should depend on AP-1 (dominant-negative FOS/TAM67 or c-Jun degron).

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 footprinting
description: Run ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN and H3K27ac before stimulation, after stimulation, and after resolution. Test whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers remain open or primed after AP-1 has left; persistent accessibility at sites opened by AP-1 is the key readout.

title: Acute degron depletion after the initial stimulus
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron on JUN or FOS and remove the protein either during the priming stimulus or only during the maintenance period. If memory needs AP-1 only to establish it, removal during priming abolishes it and removal later does not. If AP-1 is also needed to maintain it, both abolish it. This separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Single-cell live reporters and lineage tracking
description: Image AP-1 activity reporters (e.g., a FOS-GFP knock-in or an AP-1 response-element reporter) and track cell lineages through divisions after a pulse. Test whether activity states are inherited by daughter cells more than expected from random sibling pairing, and use single-cell multiome data to link state heritability to chromatin.

title: Synthetic AP-1 pulse sufficiency test with locus-specific perturbation
description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic JUN/FOS activation with defined pulse numbers, durations and frequencies, and measure persistence of target gene expression and accessibility. Then use dCas9 to block AP-1 sites at one enhancer to test that site's necessity. Together these show whether AP-1 dynamics alone are sufficient to establish a lasting state, and whether the memory is stored at specific loci.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge (priming assay)
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or wounding), wait days to weeks after FOS/JUN levels return to baseline, then re-stimulate and compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq) against naive cells. Include AP-1 inhibitors (e.g., T-5224) or dominant-negative FOS (A-FOS) present only during the first stimulus to test whether AP-1 is needed to establish the memory.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 footprinting
description: Run ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag for AP-1 factors and H3K27ac at time points before, during and long after the stimulus. Test whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay open after the AP-1 proteins have left, and whether they are the same loci that show the primed response. Also test whether AP-1 binding is interleaved with other pioneer or chromatin factors that keep sites open.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and pulse history
description: Use endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or AP-1 reporters in single cells and deliver stimulus pulses that vary in number and spacing. Test whether earlier pulses change later response amplitude (hysteresis), and whether the response is cell-autonomous and inherited by daughter cells after division.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory-specific enhancers after the initial stimulus
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 or motif mutation at candidate AP-1-dependent enhancers only after the initial stimulus, and optionally use acute degron tags (dTAG) to remove AP-1 at defined times. If AP-1 maintains memory continuously, late depletion should erase it; if AP-1 only establishes memory, late depletion should not. This separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Mathematical modeling and bistability tests
description: Build a model of AP-1 feedback (e.g., JUN autoregulation, with chromatin states) and fit it to dose-response and washout data. Test its predictions of bistability, a threshold dose for memory, and a hysteresis loop using dose titration and cell sorting by AP-1 level, looking for small stimulus changes that switch the system between stable states.

title: Persistence of chromatin accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells briefly (e.g., TPA, TNF, or wounding), then profile ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN days to weeks after withdrawal. AP-1-motif-enriched open sites that remain accessible after AP-1 occupancy is lost would indicate a memory of the stimulus.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 during priming vs. recall phases
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degradation of c-JUN/FOS (or dominant-negative A-FOS) only during the priming stimulus, only during the maintenance interval, or only during restimulation. Comparing secondary transcriptional responses separates AP-1 as the initiator of memory (needed at priming) from the reader or maintainer (needed later).

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of AP-1 activity and memory-gene response
description: Pair live-cell AP-1 reporters or single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with repeated stimulation to correlate each cell's first-pulse AP-1 dynamics with its second-pulse response. Test whether AP-1 dose and duration predict a heritable, cell-autonomous response bias, including through cell division by lineage tracing.

title: Motif-mutation and dCas9 perturbation of AP-1 sites at memory loci
description: At candidate memory enhancers, use CRISPR base editing to mutate AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-KRAB/p300 to silence or activate specific enhancers, and test whether the primed chromatin state (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, accessibility) and faster re-induction are lost. To test sufficiency, force AP-1 binding there with a synthetic recruiter and test whether memory is created without the stimulus.

title: BAF remodeler dependence and histone mark kinetics after an AP-1 pulse
description: Perform time-resolved ChIP or CUT&Tag for SWI/SNF (BRG1/ARID1A), H3K27ac and H3K4me1 after an AP-1 pulse, and inhibit or degrade BAF during the memory interval. If AP-1 only initiates and remodelers keep sites open, accessibility should collapse when they are removed; this tests whether memory resides in AP-1 itself or in the chromatin states it establishes.

title: Prior-stimulus re-challenge assay with acute AP-1 degradation
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, growth factor, or stress), rest them for days, then re-stimulate and measure transcription kinetics (nascent RNA-seq/PRO-seq) of AP-1 targets versus naive cells. Faster or stronger induction that depends on the first exposure, and that disappears when AP-1 (e.g., c-Fos/c-Jun) is acutely degraded during the rest period, would indicate AP-1-dependent memory.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy tracking
description: Run ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for Fos/Jun family members, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) before stimulation, after it, and after a long washout. Check whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 is no longer bound to them, which would show that AP-1 leaves a lasting chromatin imprint, and compare with enhancers that revert.

title: Acute degron perturbation at defined time windows
description: Use dTAG/auxin degrons on JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-Fos, applied only during the initial stimulus, only during the maintenance period, or only at recall. This separates AP-1's role in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it or reading it out, with persistence of accessibility and recall transcription as readouts.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and heritability
description: Track endogenously tagged Fos/Jun and an AP-1 reporter in single cells through stimulation, washout, and cell divisions. Test whether past activity predicts later responsiveness, and whether sister cells inherit similar states. Fit bistability or hysteresis models, such as feed-forward Jun autoregulation, to see if sustained states persist without the stimulus.

title: Enhancer-specific necessity and sufficiency tests for AP-1
description: Mutate or CRISPR-dCas9-block AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and conversely tether AP-1 or chromatin-remodeler recruiters (e.g., BAF) to them by CRISPR. Then measure whether recall expression and the epigenetic state are lost or gained. Necessity of the motif and sufficiency of tethering without stimulus would be the strongest causal evidence.

title: Pulse-chase of AP-1 accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Give a brief stimulus (e.g., TNF, wounding cytokine, or PMA) and map chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) ChIP/CUT&RUN at days 0, 1, 7, 21 after withdrawal. Persistent AP-1-bound open sites after signal loss would show an epigenetic trace; a faster secondary response at those loci would show it is functional.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) c-JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS induced only after the priming stimulus is gone, then re-stimulate. If the enhanced transcriptional response disappears, AP-1 is needed to maintain memory and not only to establish it. Compare with degradation only during priming to separate establishment from maintenance.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 reporter history
description: Image AP-1 activity reporters or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN in single cells through repeated stimulus pulses, and track lineages. Quantify whether the prior response predicts later amplitude or kinetics and whether the state is inherited by daughter cells, which distinguishes cell-autonomous memory from population heterogeneity.

title: Chromatin context and cofactor cooperation at memory loci
description: Profile H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and DNA methylation, together with pioneer factor and SWI/SNF (BAF) occupancy, at AP-1 sites that stay open. Perturb the cofactors or the AP-1 motif by CRISPR, and test whether the site is self-sustaining (AP-1 recruits remodelers that keep the site accessible) or a passive mark.

title: Sufficiency test by synthetic AP-1 pulse and motif editing
description: Drive AP-1 optogenetically or chemogenetically with defined durations and doses in naive cells, and measure whether transient AP-1 alone leaves lasting accessibility and enhanced re-induction. Pair this with CRISPR deletion or mutation of individual AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers to test necessity at the locus level.

title: Transient stimulus then washout: persistence of AP-1 chromatin accessibility
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or keratinocytes) to a defined pulse of TPA, TNF or wounding signal, remove it, and track ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN, and H3K27ac at AP-1 motif sites over days to weeks. Memory is supported if accessibility and a faster, stronger transcriptional response to restimulation persist after signaling and AP-1 levels return to baseline. A second exposure is expected to differ from the first.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate maintenance from initiation
description: Use dTAG or auxin-degron alleles of FOS, JUNB or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) at different times: before priming, during the memory phase, and just before restimulation. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, then removing it later spares the primed response. If it is needed throughout, then removing it later erases the primed response, which indicates a maintenance role.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage barcoding across divisions
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC on barcoded clonal lineages after priming and after several cell divisions. Test whether sister cells share AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR deviation scores) and restimulation responses more than unrelated cells do. This tests whether the state is heritable rather than due to long-lived protein or persistent signaling.

title: Live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and reporter memory
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN and use an AP-1 target-locus reporter in live single cells during repeated stimulation pulses. Quantify how the history of AP-1 dynamics (pulse number, interval) predicts later reporter output and speed of reactivation. Compare with mathematical models of bistability or hysteresis, and check for a persistent self-reinforcing loop.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and sufficiency tests at AP-1 sites
description: Use dCas9 to recruit or block AP-1 at specific primed enhancers, or mutate the motifs, with CRISPRi/a and base editing. Then test whether deposited marks and the primed response last without the original stimulus. Pair this with Hi-C or Micro-C to see whether AP-1-dependent enhancer–promoter contacts carry the memory, testing whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient and not merely correlated.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge and first-pulse AP-1 loss
description: Give cells a defined first pulse of a stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or injury cue), rest them for varying intervals, then re-stimulate. Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, nascent RNA) with naive cells to test whether AP-1 history changes the second response and how long the change lasts. Include AP-1 loss (dominant-negative FOS/A-Fos, or degron) during the first pulse only, to test whether AP-1 is needed to set the memory.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy mapping
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN or CUT&Tag for JUN/FOS, and H3K27ac at time points before, during and after the stimulus, through to weeks after it is withdrawn. Look for AP-1 motif sites that stay open or primed after AP-1 itself has left, then test whether those sites predict the stronger or faster second response.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and persistence
description: Track endogenously tagged FOS/JUN, or an AP-1 reporter, in single cells over repeated stimulations, using lineage tracing across divisions. Measure whether past AP-1 activity level, duration, or pulse pattern in a cell or its ancestors predicts the later response. This separates memory carried by cell state from population-level noise.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory-site enhancers
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 or motif deletion at specific AP-1-dependent memory enhancers, either before the first stimulus or only between stimuli. If memory requires the site to be primed, silencing it before the first pulse should block memory, whereas silencing it afterward tests whether the site must be actively maintained. Add a gain-of-function arm, with synthetic AP-1 recruitment (dCas9-FOS) to a naive locus to test whether it can install memory.

title: Testing the maintenance mechanism: epigenetic and feedback contributions
description: Test whether memory persists through chromatin remodelers (BAF/SWI-SNF), histone marks, or positive feedback of AP-1 on its own expression by inhibiting each during the rest period and measuring loss of the primed state. Use mathematical modelling of bistable or hysteretic AP-1 circuits to distinguish these mechanisms. In vivo, compare AP-1 conditional knockouts with controls on repeat injury in regenerating or injured skin.

title: Hysteresis of AP-1 target expression with dominant-negative control
description: Titrate a transient AP-1 stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or PMA/ligand-induced c-Fos/c-Jun) up and then down, and measure target gene expression and AP-1 occupancy at each dose. A down-sweep that differs from the up-sweep at identical input (path dependence) would show bistability and memory; compare with AP-1 dominant-negative (A-Fos) cells, which should lose this difference.

title: Fos-driven permanent labeling of previously activated cells
description: Use a Fos-driven Cre-ER/TRAP-style reporter to permanently label cells that experienced a prior AP-1 activation event, then re-stimulate days to weeks later. Compare transcriptional response and chromatin accessibility between labeled and unlabeled cells by single-cell multiome; faster, stronger, or qualitatively different responses in labeled cells would indicate AP-1-dependent priming memory.

title: Lineage-based autocorrelation of AP-1 activity across cell divisions
description: Perform time-lapse imaging of live AP-1 reporters in single cells with lineage tracing across divisions, then compute the autocorrelation of AP-1 activity between mothers, daughters and cousins, as in heritability estimates. Inheritance of activity state after a transient pulse beyond what shared environment explains would quantify mitotic memory and its decay half-life.

title: Mitotic chromatin profiling of AP-1 with acute degron depletion
description: Perform CUT&Tag/ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and enhancer marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) in mitotically arrested versus interphase cells after a prior stimulation, to test whether AP-1 stays bound to or leaves persistent accessible sites at specific loci. Pair this with acute dTAG-mediated depletion of AP-1 after the stimulus to test whether maintaining accessibility requires continued AP-1 presence or only its initial pioneering.

title: Modeling and perturbing the AP-1 autoregulatory loop
description: Build a mathematical model of the AP-1 autoregulatory loop (FOS/JUN promoters containing TRE sites), then test its predictions by breaking the loop (CRISPR mutation of TREs, inducible degrons at varied timing) and measuring whether the active state persists, collapses, or can be reset. Distinguish feedback-based from chromatin-based memory by comparing persistence after degron removal at early versus late times.

title: Hysteresis in AP-1 occupancy and target expression under ramped stimulus
description: Expose cells to a ramped-up then ramped-down stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or chemically controlled FOS/JUN input) and measure AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) and target gene expression along both paths. A non-overlapping up/down response, with residual signal at zero stimulus, would indicate path-dependent memory attributable to AP-1.

title: Prime–rest–rechallenge with AP-1 degron and PRO-seq
description: Give cells a first stimulus, rest them for variable intervals, then re-stimulate, measuring faster or stronger transcription at primed loci by nascent RNA-seq (PRO-seq). Acutely degrade AP-1 factors (dTAG) only during priming versus only during re-stimulation to separate AP-1's role in establishing versus retrieving memory.

title: AP-1-driven Cre or recorder tagging of past AP-1 activity
description: Use an AP-1-driven Cre or recorder (analogous to FOS-driven TRAP) to permanently tag cells that experienced AP-1 activation. Compare tagged and untagged sibling cells for later chromatin accessibility (scATAC) and response to re-stimulation, to test whether past AP-1 activity predicts durable, cell-autonomous state differences.

title: Persistence-time analysis from single-cell live imaging
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a transcription reporter in single cells over days, then fit autocorrelation and mutual-information decay times. Compare these decay times with AP-1 protein half-life and chromatin mark half-life to test whether persistence exceeds what protein turnover alone explains.

title: Persistence of AP-1-opened enhancers after AP-1 removal
description: Test whether AP-1 opens enhancers that remain accessible after AP-1 is removed. Perform time-course ATAC-seq, H3K27ac ChIP and motif analysis after stimulus withdrawal, and use dCas9-based tethering of AP-1 or motif mutation at selected enhancers to test whether persistent accessibility is AP-1-dependent and whether it is sufficient to enhance later responses.

title: Stimulus up-and-down titration to test hysteresis in AP-1 and chromatin accessibility
description: Titrate a stimulus (e.g., TPA, growth factor, or stress) up and then down, and measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) levels and chromatin accessibility at target enhancers by single-cell ATAC/CUT&Tag at matched doses on each branch. Path-dependent output at identical input, persisting after the stimulus is removed, would indicate memory rather than simple tracking of the input.

title: Prime-rest-challenge design with AP-1 loss during priming or recall
description: Give cells a primary stimulus, rest them for days to weeks, then give a secondary challenge and compare transcription kinetics and magnitude with naive cells. Measure AP-1 occupancy and H3K27ac at primed enhancers by time-course ChIP/CUT&RUN, and test whether AP-1 loss (dominant-negative A-FOS or degron) only during priming, or only during recall, abolishes the faster or larger secondary response.

title: Testing AP-1 positive autoregulation as a bistable switch
description: Treat AP-1 positive autoregulation (JUN/FOS promoters bound by AP-1) as a candidate bistable switch. Use live-cell reporters of endogenous FOS/JUN and optogenetic or chemically induced pulses of varied duration to look for threshold behavior, bimodal single-cell distributions, and persistence of the ON state. Then mutate the AP-1 sites in the promoter to test whether memory is lost.

title: Inheritance of AP-1 state across cell divisions and mitotic bookmarking
description: Use time-lapse imaging of AP-1 reporters in sister and cousin cells after a transient stimulus to measure how the state is inherited, with correlation expected to decay with generational distance. Also use mitotic-chromosome CUT&Tag and live imaging to test whether AP-1 stays on chromatin through mitosis (bookmarking) and whether the memory persists across divisions.

title: Order-dependent AP-1 enhancer accessibility after sequential stimuli
description: Apply sequential stimuli (A then B, or the reverse order) and map which AP-1 motif-containing enhancers become newly accessible. Use footprinting, motif-resolved ATAC and Hi-C/Micro-C to identify sites established by the first stimulus that persist after AP-1 is removed. Test sufficiency by recruiting AP-1 to the site with dCas9 in naive cells to see whether it recreates the remembered state.

title: Hysteresis of AP-1 occupancy, accessibility and transcription
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., serum, TNF, or Ras/ERK activity via optogenetics) up and then down, and measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy, chromatin accessibility and target transcription at matched stimulus levels. A path-dependent loop, with different output on the way up than on the way down, would indicate memory, and the loop area quantifies its strength.

title: Prime-rest-rechallenge with acute AP-1 degradation to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, rest them for varying intervals, then re-challenge. Compare ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for AP-1 and H3K27ac, and the speed and amplitude of the transcriptional response with naive cells, with and without acute AP-1 degradation (dTAG or dominant-negative A-FOS) during priming versus during recall, to separate establishment from maintenance.

title: Mutual information between past stimulus and current single-cell state
description: Use live-cell reporters of FOS/JUN dynamics and target genes in single cells, and compute mutual information between past stimulus history and current state after the stimulus ends. Memory is indicated if the state retains information about past input beyond a decay time. Compare the analysis with perturbations of AP-1 dimer composition.

title: Bistability modeling of AP-1 feedback with single-cell sorting
description: Fit a mathematical model of AP-1 binding, nucleosome opening and positive feedback (e.g., FOSL1/JUN autoregulation) to time-resolved data. Test the predicted bistability and critical stimulus thresholds by sorting ON and OFF single-cell subpopulations and tracking their persistence through cell divisions.

title: Lineage barcoding with an AP-1 activation tag to follow past AP-1 activity
description: Combine lineage barcoding with a mark of AP-1 activation (e.g., a Cre- or recorder-based AP-1-responsive tag) to record which cells experienced past AP-1 activity. Then use single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) to test whether tagged cells and their descendants keep distinct accessible AP-1 motif landscapes and expression compared with untagged siblings over many divisions.

title: Hysteresis of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility with acute degron test
description: Titrate a stimulus (e.g., FOS/JUN induction via optogenetic or dox-controlled dosing) up and then back down, measuring AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) at target enhancers. A path-dependent, non-retracing response at matched input levels would indicate AP-1-dependent memory, and acute degron removal of AP-1 would test whether the retained state requires it.

title: Prime–rest–rechallenge with memory half-life fitting
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA or a mechanical/inflammatory cue), rest them for variable intervals, then re-stimulate. Measure faster or stronger transcription of AP-1 target genes (nascent RNA, PRO-seq) and fit decay curves to estimate memory half-life, with and without dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS) during priming only.

title: Barcoded clonal inheritance of AP-1 activity
description: Use lineage barcoding with live AP-1 reporters to follow sister cells after a transient stimulus. Compute intra-clonal versus inter-clonal correlation of AP-1 activity and target gene expression across divisions, and use the heritability of the state to quantify mitotic memory.

title: Single-cell test for bistability from AP-1 positive feedback
description: Test whether AP-1, through positive autoregulation of the FOS/JUN promoters, forms a bistable switch. Use live single-cell imaging of AP-1 reporters with a scan of stimulus pulse width and amplitude to look for bimodality, a switching threshold, and persistence after the input is withdrawn. Then perturb the feedback loop (e.g., mutate AP-1 sites in the JUN promoter) to see whether bistability is lost.

title: Time-resolved multi-omics of residual enhancer states with AP-1 motif editing
description: After a stimulus is removed, perform time-course ATAC-seq, histone mark ChIP (H3K27ac, H3K4me1), and AP-1 motif-footprint analysis to define which enhancers stay in residual accessible states. Then use CRISPRi/dCas9 editing of AP-1 motifs at these sites to test causally whether the retained accessibility and the primed response of linked genes depend on the AP-1 sites.

title: Hysteresis of AP-1 chromatin state under rising and falling stimulus
description: Expose cells to a rising then falling dose of a stimulus (e.g., TPA, or optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun activation) and measure ATAC-seq accessibility and target gene expression at matched doses on both the up and down ramps. Non-overlapping up and down curves at AP-1 motif-containing enhancers, persisting after AP-1 levels return to baseline, would indicate memory rather than simple tracking of the input.

title: Spaced versus massed optogenetic AP-1 pulses
description: Deliver optogenetic AP-1 pulses with the same total dose either massed or spaced, then challenge cells days later with a weak stimulus. Compare the secondary response (transcription, accessibility) between the two regimes to test whether AP-1 encodes stimulus history and shows learning-like kinetics.

title: Lineage barcoding to test heritable AP-1-linked states
description: Tag individual cells with heritable barcodes, expose the population to a transient stimulus, and track clonal lineages with single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) plus AP-1 footprinting. Test whether sister cells share AP-1-linked accessibility and expression states over multiple divisions, and whether the shared state predicts later responsiveness, to distinguish heritable memory from stochastic noise.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different times after priming
description: Prime cells, then acutely degrade AP-1 (dTAG or auxin degron on c-Jun or FOSL) at different times after priming. If primed accessibility and enhanced re-induction persist without AP-1, the memory is stored elsewhere (e.g., in histone marks); if the memory decays, AP-1 is required for maintenance and not only initiation. Use CUT&RUN for H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and AP-1 binding to map what remains.

title: Single-cell time-lapse and modeling of AP-1 bistability
description: Use live reporters of AP-1 activity (e.g., a Fos-GFP knock-in or synthetic AP-1 reporter) in single cells after transient stimulation, and fit ODE or Bayesian models to the dynamics to test for bimodal, self-sustaining states. Perturb feedback nodes (FOS/JUN autoregulation, MAPK inhibition) to test whether memory arises from the positive-feedback circuit, and compare model predictions with held-out perturbations.

title: Hysteresis of AP-1 target expression and accessibility
description: Expose cells to a ramping-up then ramping-down stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or ERK/JNK activation driving FOS/JUN) and measure single-cell AP-1 target expression and chromatin accessibility on both paths. Non-overlapping up and down curves, with residual response after the stimulus returns to zero, would show state-dependent memory rather than simple input tracking.

title: Perturbation-recovery and tipping-point analysis of AP-1 activity
description: Apply pulses of varying strength and duration to cells and track recovery time and variance of AP-1 activity using live FOS/JUN reporters. Increasing recovery time near a threshold and bimodal persistence of the primed state would indicate bistability supporting memory.

title: AP-1 occupancy and accessibility time series through mitosis
description: Map AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy and accessibility at enhancers by ChIP/CUT&Tag and ATAC-seq days after stimulus withdrawal and through cell division (mitotic versus interphase chromosomes). Sites that remain open and AP-1-bound, and that respond faster on restimulation, would mark AP-1-dependent memory loci.

title: Prime-rest-boost design with stage-specific AP-1 degradation
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then give a second challenge and compare transcriptional kinetics and amplitude with naive cells. Acutely degrade AP-1 factors (dTAG/auxin) or express dominant-negative A-FOS only during priming, only during rest, or only during the second challenge, to determine whether AP-1 is needed to establish, maintain, or read out memory.

title: Synthetic AP-1 site reporter to test sufficiency for stable ON state
description: Insert a reporter flanked by wild-type versus mutated AP-1 motifs (or use dCas9 recruitment of FOS/JUN) and test whether a transient stimulus pulse yields a stable ON state over many divisions, read out by flow cytometry and single-cell lineage tracking. Include a control without pioneer factor and a BAF chromatin remodeler inhibitor to test whether AP-1 alone is sufficient to maintain the state.

title: Hysteresis loops of AP-1 binding, accessibility and transcription per locus
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or titrated FOS/JUN induction or MAPK activity) up and then down, and measure AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target transcription at matched input levels. A non-overlapping up/down response that persists after the stimulus is removed would indicate history-dependent memory, and the loop width could be quantified per locus.

title: Prime–rest–rechallenge with stage-specific AP-1 inhibition
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (priming), allow a defined rest period, then rechallenge. Compare the kinetics and amplitude of target gene induction and AP-1 occupancy in primed versus naive cells. Give AP-1 dominant-negative (e.g., A-FOS) only during priming or only during rechallenge to separate AP-1's role in establishing versus executing memory.

title: Barcoded lineage split-clone test of AP-1 state heritability
description: Use barcoded lineages with a split-clone design: stimulate one sister arm and not the other, then use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) to test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target gene expression are more similar among sisters and across divisions than among unrelated cells. Estimate the heritability of the state across generations to determine whether it is mitotically stable.

title: Dynamical model and live reporters to test AP-1 bistability
description: Build a dynamical-systems model of AP-1 with positive feedback (FOS/JUN autoregulation, with cooperating pioneer factors) and fit it to single-cell trajectories from live reporters (a fluorescent AP-1 reporter and endogenous FOS-tagged knock-ins). Test model predictions of bistability: bimodal distributions, critical slowing down near thresholds, and state switching after brief pulses. Then perturb the feedback loops to see whether memory is lost.

title: Locus-level perturbation and timed degron tests of AP-1 maintenance versus initiation
description: After stimulation is removed and the state has been set, use dCas9-based degradation or motif mutation at selected AP-1 sites. Measure whether neighboring chromatin marks (H3K27ac, accessibility) and gene expression persist, collapse, or are rebuilt. Combine with timed AP-1 dTAG degron experiments to determine whether continuous AP-1 presence is required to maintain the state or whether AP-1 only initiates a self-sustaining state.

title: Timed AP-1 degradation after priming with counter-perturbation
description: Acutely degrade or inhibit AP-1 (e.g., dTAG degron of FOS/JUN, dominant-negative A-FOS) at different times after a priming stimulus, then quantify chromatin accessibility and transcriptional response on restimulation. Compare this with a counter-perturbation that boosts the opposing factors, to show that AP-1 is needed specifically to maintain the primed state and not just to induce it.

title: Pulse-train stimulation with live AP-1 reporters
description: Test how AP-1 responds to pulsed versus sustained stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or growth factor pulses of varied frequency and spacing). Track FOS/JUN dynamics live with endogenous knock-in reporters, and test whether the response to a second pulse depends on the interval since the first. A decay time constant lasting days after the stimulus is gone would support memory.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of AP-1 motif accessibility across a prime–rest–restimulate time course
description: Run scATAC-seq and RNA-seq at baseline, after priming, after a long rest, and after restimulation. Use chromVAR and footprinting to determine whether AP-1 sites opened by priming stay open during rest and whether they predict faster or stronger gene induction. Link this to lineage barcodes to separate heritable memory across divisions from persistence in non-dividing cells.

title: Memory persistence through cell division
description: Follow primed cells through a defined number of divisions using dye dilution or a division-tracking reporter. Measure AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN) and the primed response after 0, 1, 2 and more divisions. Test whether memory halves with each division, indicating dilution, or is stably re-established, indicating a self-propagating mechanism.

title: Sufficiency test with AP-1 motif editing and transient dCas9-FOS/JUN recruitment
description: Use CRISPR to mutate or insert AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers, or to transiently recruit dCas9–FOS/JUN, then remove the trigger. Measure whether enhancer accessibility, H3K27ac, and enhanced gene induction persist after AP-1 is gone. Persistence would show AP-1 can write memory, and loss of memory when only the motifs are mutated would show the sites are necessary.

title: Decoding AP-1 pulse patterns with live-cell reporters
description: Image live-cell AP-1 reporters (e.g., FOS/JUN-tagged or AP-1 transcriptional reporters) after transient stimuli of different duration and frequency. Test whether pulse pattern, not just amplitude, is encoded and whether it predicts later gene expression and cell fate, and compare with single-cell memory of the pattern after a washout period.

title: Priming and rechallenge with AP-1 degron
description: Give cells a first stimulus (e.g., growth factor, TPA, or inflammatory cue), rest them for days, then rechallenge and measure the enhanced or altered transcriptional response by RNA-seq. Use an acute degron (dTAG/auxin) on FOS/JUN family members during priming only versus rechallenge only, to separate AP-1 needed to establish the memory from AP-1 needed to read it.

title: Time-course profiling of AP-1 sites that stay accessible
description: Run ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 motifs, H3K27ac, and BAF/pioneer markers before, after, and long after stimulus to find enhancers that stay open after AP-1 levels return to baseline. Test whether persistence depends on AP-1 motif integrity using CRISPR motif mutation or dCas9 interference at selected enhancers.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC sequencing with a lineage barcode in stimulated and unstimulated populations, and measure whether sister cells share AP-1 target accessibility and expression states after multiple divisions. Quantify heritability as sister-cell correlation versus random pairs, and whether it decays, to distinguish epigenetic memory from persistent signaling.

title: Transient AP-1 induction and positive-feedback mapping
description: Use optogenetic or inducible pulses of c-Jun/c-Fos in naive cells and test whether a self-sustaining state emerges by measuring endogenous JUN/FOS autoregulation, target gene persistence and enhancer state weeks later. Perturb the loop (mutate AP-1 sites in the JUN promoter, block signaling kinases such as JNK) to determine whether memory requires feedback or continuing upstream input.

title: Decoding of stimulus temporal patterns by AP-1
description: Stimulate cells with pulsed versus sustained signals (optogenetic or ERK/JNK-activating pulses of defined count and interval) and measure FOS/JUN live-reporter dynamics and downstream gene sets. Test whether distinct temporal patterns produce distinct, persistent chromatin and transcriptional states, which would indicate the pattern is stored and not just transiently read.

title: Minimal set of persistently accessible AP-1-bound enhancers
description: Use single-cell CUT&Tag/ATAC-seq to identify the minimal set of AP-1-bound enhancers that stay accessible after the stimulus ends. Compare accessibility, AP-1 motif occupancy and H3K27ac at these sites days after a transient stimulus versus in naive cells, and test whether this reduced set suffices to predict the primed response.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined times after stimulus
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degradation of FOS/JUN family members or dominant-negative A-FOS at different times after the priming stimulus. If memory persists after AP-1 removal, AP-1 only initiates it; if secondary responses and accessibility collapse, AP-1 actively maintains it. Compare these outcomes across timepoints.

title: Dual readout of memory: re-stimulation response and persistent chromatin marks
description: In the same cells, compare the faster, stronger transcriptional response on re-stimulation (RNA-seq/nascent PRO-seq) with the persistent chromatin marks present without stimulation. Correlate the two per locus and per cell, and test causality by CRISPR mutation of AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers to see whether both readouts are lost together.

title: Lineage tracing of memory across divisions with mitotic bookmarking assays
description: Track primed cells through multiple cell cycles with live AP-1/target reporters and barcoded lineages or sister-cell comparisons, measuring how many divisions the primed state lasts and whether sisters inherit it equally. Combine this with mitotic-bookmarking assays (live imaging and mitotic ChIP) to test whether AP-1 stays bound to chromatin through mitosis, and use decay-rate modelling to separate heritable memory from slowly decaying signaling.

title: Minimal chromatin footprint of AP-1 memory elements
description: Use CUT&Tag/ATAC-seq plus motif-mutant and dCas9-based perturbations to identify which AP-1-bound enhancer elements (c-Jun/Fos occupancy, H3K27ac, BAF-dependent accessibility) persist after stimulus removal. Then test whether this minimal set is necessary and sufficient for faster re-induction of target genes.

title: Prime–rest–restimulate with acute AP-1 degradation
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TNF, EGF, or wounding signals), wait varying rest periods, and restimulate, measuring the transcriptional response by nascent RNA-seq. Use dTAG/auxin degrons on FOS/JUN during priming, during rest, or during restimulation to determine whether AP-1 is needed to establish, maintain, or read out the memory.

title: Live-cell decoding of AP-1 pulse dynamics
description: Test whether AP-1 encodes stimulation history in its temporal pattern. Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and AP-1 reporters in single cells under optogenetic or microfluidic pulses of varied frequency and duration, then relate prior pulse patterns to later response amplitude and persistence using information-theoretic measures.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Pair single-cell ATAC+RNA with lineage barcodes to follow sister cells after transient stimulation. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR) and target expression are shared among clonal relatives more than expected and persist across divisions, which would indicate heritable memory, compared with transient states.

title: Bistability and hysteresis in a synthetic AP-1 circuit
description: Build a synthetic or engineered positive-feedback AP-1 locus, such as a JUN autoregulatory loop, and measure input–output curves in forward and reverse dose sweeps to detect hysteresis. Fit mathematical models and perturb feedback (mutate the JUN promoter TRE site, block pioneering cofactors) to test whether AP-1 feedback is required for self-sustaining states.

title: AP-1 dynamics as a temporal code for chromatin state
description: Drive cells with optogenetic or chemically gated ERK/JNK pulses of varied frequency and duration, and live-image FOS/JUN reporters. Test whether pulse pattern, not just total dose, determines distinct downstream chromatin states and gene programs that persist after stimulation stops.

title: Chromatin-accessibility memory after transient stimulation
description: Stimulate cells once, wash out, and perform ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN, FOSL) and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at days 0, 1, 7, and 14 compared with naive cells. Persistent AP-1-bound, accessible primed enhancers that give faster or stronger re-induction on second stimulation would indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance of memory
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the first stimulus or only after the memory is established. If depletion during priming abolishes the later re-response but depletion afterward does not, AP-1 is needed to establish the memory; if later depletion also erases it, AP-1 is needed to maintain it.

title: Single-cell prime-and-rechallenge with lineage tracing
description: Prime cells, let them divide, and perform single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with barcoded lineage tracking to test whether sister cells share AP-1 motif accessibility and response magnitude to a second challenge. Heritable clonal concordance of response, correlated with AP-1 occupancy, would indicate mitotically stable memory rather than transient signaling.

title: Targeted enhancer perturbation: necessity and sufficiency of AP-1 binding
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 or motif mutation to silence or edit AP-1 binding sites at candidate memory enhancers, and tether AP-1 (dCas9-FOS/JUN) to naive loci. Measure whether the edits eliminate or create faster re-induction of the nearby gene, to test necessity and sufficiency of AP-1 binding for locus-specific memory.

title: Hysteresis test with graded stimulus dose and withdrawal
description: Stimulate cells with a graded dose series of a stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or growth factor), then withdraw it, and measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene expression on the rising and falling arms. If AP-1 encodes memory, accessibility and expression should depend on stimulus history (hysteresis) and not just follow the current input.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after the priming stimulus
description: After a priming stimulus, remove AP-1 with a degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS at different times, either during priming or after it has ended. Then re-stimulate and compare the secondary response. This separates AP-1 as initiator of memory from AP-1 as maintainer, and shows whether the memory state persists without continuous AP-1 occupancy.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of synchrony and heritability
description: Combine live-cell AP-1 reporters or FOS/JUN imaging with lineage tracing across cell divisions and with single-cell RNA plus ATAC. This tests whether primed cells pass their state to daughter cells and whether neighboring cells synchronize through paracrine signals. It also tests whether memory is a bimodal cell-intrinsic state or a population average.

title: AP-1 pioneer-like activity and epigenetic coupling at new enhancers
description: Do time-course CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for AP-1 subunits, H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and BAF/SWI-SNF components, and measure nucleosome occupancy with ATAC footprinting at newly opened enhancers. Test whether the enhancers stay open and marked after AP-1 leaves, and whether motif mutation by CRISPR base editing removes the memory at that site only.

title: Feedback-loop modeling and perturbation of AP-1 positive feedback
description: Build a dynamical model of AP-1 positive feedback, in which FOS/JUN transcription drives further AP-1 activity through autoregulation and signaling loops, and fit it to time-resolved data on protein levels and phosphorylation (JNK/ERK). Then test the model's predictions of bistability and a critical stimulus threshold by perturbing feedback nodes optogenetically or with inhibitors, to determine whether memory persists as a self-sustaining state.

title: Identifying the minimal AP-1 features required for memory
description: Use domain-specific mutants of FOS/JUN (DNA-binding, dimerization, and pioneer-like or chromatin-remodeler recruitment domains) to test which element is required for a stimulus-induced chromatin accessibility state to persist after the stimulus is removed. Measure persistence by ATAC-seq and H3K27ac CUT&Tag over several cell divisions.

title: Stimulus-withdrawal time course with timed acute AP-1 degradation
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TPA, wounding signals, or inflammatory cues), then withdraw the stimulus. Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) to remove AP-1 factors during priming only, after washout only, or both, and measure enhancer accessibility, AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) and target gene re-inducibility to separate AP-1 as an initiator from AP-1 as a maintainer of the memory.

title: Pulse-pattern dependence of memory writing
description: Deliver identical total stimulus doses with different on/off patterns (e.g., 2 h on, 6 h off versus continuous) using optogenetic or chemically inducible FOS/JUN, and read out with live-cell AP-1 reporters and single-cell RNA-seq or ATAC-seq. This tests whether AP-1 dynamics, not just level, determine whether a durable memory is written and how strongly secondary stimulation is primed.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory inheritance
description: Mark cells with a live AP-1 reporter or endogenous tagged FOS/JUN and a heritable barcode. After transient stimulation, follow sister cells through division and test whether the AP-1 state and accessible chromatin are shared more between sisters than between random cells. Then compare the restimulation response of memory-positive and memory-negative sister lineages, and use the results to model mitotic bookmarking and inheritance.

title: Targeted addition and removal of AP-1 sites at specific enhancers
description: Use dCas9-based recruitment, or deletion/mutation of AP-1 motifs, at candidate memory enhancers (e.g., near genes with faster second responses). Test whether adding AP-1 sites is sufficient to create a primed, faster-responding state and whether removing them abolishes it, without altering the global stimulus. Measure local accessibility, histone marks, nascent transcription (PRO-seq), and secondary-response kinetics to establish site-specific causality.

title: Identifying minimal AP-1 sites and enhancers required for memory
description: Perform ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN after a transient stimulus and after washout to identify persistently accessible AP-1-bound enhancers. Then use CRISPR deletion or dCas9-KRAB at these sites to test which are necessary for a heightened secondary response.

title: Prime-rest-restimulate time course with AP-1 perturbation
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts) once, rest them for days, then restimulate and measure transcriptional output by RNA-seq and nascent RNA. Compare primed with naive cells under dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS) or acute degron-mediated JUN/FOS depletion applied only during priming versus only during restimulation, to separate AP-1 needed to establish memory from AP-1 needed to read it.

title: Live single-cell AP-1 reporters for pulse-pattern history
description: Test whether AP-1 activity dynamics (pulse number, duration, frequency) encode and store stimulation history. Use live-cell FOS/JUN knock-in fluorescent reporters with optogenetic or pulsed stimulation of defined patterns, then relate pulse history to later response and to chromatin state in the same cells.

title: Bistability and hysteresis test of the AP-1 positive-feedback loop
description: Test whether AP-1 maintains its state through self-reinforcement by titrating stimulus up and then down and measuring single-cell JUN/FOS levels by flow cytometry or imaging. A history-dependent, bimodal response (hysteresis) would indicate a self-sustaining state; mathematical modeling and disruption of the feedback loop, such as mutating AP-1 sites in the JUN promoter, would test the mechanism.

title: Persistence and inheritance of AP-1-associated memory across cell division
description: Test whether memory outlasts the signal and is passed through mitosis by tracking sorted primed cells and their daughters over several divisions. Measure AP-1 occupancy, H3K27ac, and BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment, and compare with the half-lives of AP-1 proteins and mRNAs. Persistent accessibility without AP-1 would indicate AP-1 triggers a chromatin-based memory, while loss of memory when AP-1 is removed would indicate AP-1 itself carries it.

title: Single-event monitoring of AP-1 binding dynamics
description: Use live-cell single-molecule tracking or CUT&Tag time courses to detect individual FOS/JUN binding and dwell events at specific enhancers after a transient stimulus. Test whether residence times and occupancy at 'memory' sites remain altered days after the stimulus ends, compared with naive cells.

title: Probing latent AP-1 state with a small standardized re-stimulation
description: Measure how cells respond to a small standardized re-stimulation at various times after a priming stimulus, reading out AP-1 target transcription, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and FOS/JUN levels. A faster or stronger response in primed cells that depends on AP-1 sites would indicate a stored state not visible at baseline.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different times after priming
description: Prime cells, then remove AP-1 using a degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS during priming, during the memory interval, or only at re-challenge. Compare which windows abolish the enhanced secondary response and persistent accessibility, to separate AP-1 as initiator from AP-1 as maintainer of memory.

title: AP-1 motif mutagenesis with single-cell heterogeneity analysis
description: Use CRISPR editing or base editing of individual AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, together with single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC), to determine which sites carry the memory. Test whether memory is lost per site and whether cell-to-cell heterogeneity of retained accessibility predicts the strength of the later response and its inheritance through divisions.

title: Lineage tracing of memory through cell divisions with chromatin mark analysis
description: Track primed cells and their daughters by live imaging with AP-1 reporters or barcoded lineages, and test whether elevated accessibility and reporter state persist across several generations without ongoing stimulus. Pair this with measurements of histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) and DNA methylation at AP-1 sites to identify the maintenance mechanism, and compare with cells in which division is blocked.

title: Systematic mapping of AP-1 states across stimulus histories
description: Expose cells to a grid of stimulus histories varying dose, duration, and order of pulses (e.g., TNF, EGF, or TPA). Measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN family) occupancy by CUT&RUN and chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq, then test whether the final state depends on the path taken, which would indicate memory.

title: Test of whether AP-1 memory requires active maintenance
description: After a priming stimulus and a rest period, acutely remove AP-1 using a FOS/JUN degron or dominant-negative A-FOS, and test whether primed enhancers lose accessibility and the faster secondary transcription. If memory is lost when AP-1 is removed during the rest period, it is actively maintained by AP-1. If it persists, it is held by other factors.

title: Paired live-cell imaging of primed and naive cells
description: Build a live-cell reporter of AP-1 activity, for example an AP-1 response element driving a fluorescent protein together with a tagged JUN. Follow single cells through priming, rest and restimulation, and compare the response of primed and naive cells. Measure how long the difference lasts and whether it is inherited by daughter cells, to distinguish true memory from a transient effect.

title: Sufficiency of ectopic AP-1 pulse for priming
description: Use optogenetic or inducible AP-1 (e.g., dox-inducible c-Jun/FOS) to give a transient pulse in naive cells in place of the natural stimulus. Test whether the pulse alone converts enhancers to a persistent accessible state with H3K27ac and H3K4me1 and enhances later gene induction, and compare with a mutant lacking its DNA-binding or transactivation domain.

title: Single-cell multiome with AP-1 motif perturbation
description: Perform paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq on primed and unprimed cells, using CRISPR deletion or mutation of specific AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers. Test whether motif accessibility and chromatin-state heterogeneity predict each cell's secondary response, and whether recruitment of SWI/SNF (BAF) or pioneer factors depends on those motifs, which would indicate mechanism rather than correlation.

title: Varying the interval between repeated stimulus pulses
description: Deliver repeated stimuli (e.g., TNF, wounding cues or optogenetic c-Jun/Fos) at varied intervals and measure whether chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene output at AP-1 sites on later pulses depend on the interval. A memory-like mechanism predicts a minimum recovery interval and a persistence window, whereas a transient transcription factor does not.

title: Time-resolved AP-1 occupancy and accessibility after stimulus withdrawal
description: After a priming stimulus, track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding by CUT&RUN, plus ATAC-seq and H3K27ac, at multiple time points over days to weeks, long after AP-1 activity returns to baseline. Persistently open enhancers at AP-1 motifs without sustained AP-1 binding would indicate that AP-1 established a durable epigenetic state that outlasts the signal.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during priming versus recall
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) on c-Jun/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 only during priming, only during recall (second stimulus), or during both. If memory requires AP-1 only at priming, AP-1 acts as a writer; if it is also needed at recall, AP-1 acts as a reader or maintainer.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory readout
description: Combine live-cell AP-1 reporters or FOS/JUN imaging with barcoded lineage tracing and single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC). Test whether sister cells share primed accessibility and faster re-induction, which would show heritable memory through division as opposed to a population-level transient response.

title: Motif perturbation and epigenome editing at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, and dCas9 tools to add or remove marks such as H3K27ac or DNA methylation, then measure the recall response. Loss of faster re-induction after motif mutation, with rescue by forced opening, would show necessity and sufficiency. Chromatin remodelers such as BAF could be tested as the maintenance link.

title: Bistability test of AP-1 activity via hysteresis
description: Test whether AP-1 activity is bistable by exposing cells to graded stimulus (e.g., TPA, serum, or inducible c-Fos/c-Jun) up and then down, and measuring single-cell AP-1 reporter output and target genes. Hysteresis, bimodal distributions, and persistence of the high state after stimulus removal at identical doses would indicate a self-sustaining memory state; perturbing positive feedback (c-Jun autoregulation) should abolish it.

title: Persistence of chromatin accessibility at AP-1 sites
description: Test whether transient AP-1 activation leaves lasting accessible chromatin by performing ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors, H3K27ac, and BAF remodeler occupancy at time points after stimulus washout across many cell divisions. Compare motif-defined AP-1 sites with other sites for retained accessibility and faster re-induction on restimulation.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined times after priming
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-degradable AP-1 subunit (c-Jun/FOS/FOSL) to deplete AP-1 during priming, during the memory interval, or only at restimulation. If memory requires AP-1 during the interval, depletion then should erase the faster secondary response. If only priming requires it, AP-1 acts as an initiator and the memory persists without it. Distinguish initiation from maintenance by RNA-seq and nascent transcription (PRO-seq).

title: Optogenetic pulse encoding with live reporters
description: Drive AP-1 with optogenetic or chemically timed pulses of varying duration, frequency and number while imaging a live AP-1 reporter and a target gene (e.g., MS2 or fluorescent knock-in). Fit models comparing responses of naive and pre-pulsed cells to quantify memory duration, dependence on pulse history, and whether cells integrate past inputs as a system with state.

title: Lineage-resolved single-cell multiome with memory-site mutagenesis
description: Apply single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) or barcoded lineage tracing to primed versus naive cells to test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression are inherited by sister cells beyond cell division. Then use CRISPR to mutate or dCas9-block specific AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and test whether this selectively removes the primed response while leaving other enhancers intact.

title: Persistence of individual Fos/Jun dimers at enhancers
description: Perform CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for each Fos/Jun family member before, during and after a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA or injury). Test which dimers persist at enhancers after the stimulus is gone and whether persistence predicts faster or stronger re-induction of target genes.

title: Stimulus–washout–restimulation with chromatin accessibility readout
description: Give cells a defined pulse of signal, wash it out for varying intervals, then restimulate, and measure ATAC-seq, H3K27ac and nascent transcription (PRO-seq) at AP-1 motif sites. If AP-1 acts as memory, accessibility and the transcriptional response to the second pulse should depend on the first pulse and decay with a measurable half-life.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different memory phases
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) c-Jun or Fos to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus only or during the maintenance interval only. If AP-1 is needed to establish but not maintain the memory, enhancers should stay open after removal. If it is needed for both, accessibility and re-induction should be lost, separating initiation from maintenance.

title: Live imaging of AP-1 activity with lineage tracking
description: Image an AP-1 reporter and endogenously tagged Fos/Jun in single cells and follow their progeny after a transient stimulus. Test whether the reporter state is inherited across divisions, how long it persists, and whether sister cells remain correlated, which a heritable mechanism would predict and noisy transient signaling would not.

title: Targeted perturbation of AP-1 motifs and chromatin state at individual enhancers
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs by CRISPR base editing, or recruit dCas9-based writers or erasers (p300, KRAB) to selected enhancers, then compare the primed-state response of edited and unedited alleles in the same cell. This tests whether the motif and the chromatin state it leaves are causal for memory, and whether memory acts in cis on a single allele.

title: Persistence of AP-1 binding after stimulus withdrawal
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts with TNF, TGF-β or LPS), withdraw the signal, and measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy by CUT&RUN and chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq over days to weeks. This tests whether the AP-1 binding pattern is maintained at the same enhancers after the signal is gone and persists through cell divisions.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during priming versus after memory establishment
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) c-JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the priming window or after the memory is established. If AP-1 stores the memory, removal during priming should block enhancer accessibility and faster secondary responses, while later removal should erase the memory. Measure the secondary transcriptional response by RNA-seq to distinguish AP-1's role in establishing the memory from its role in maintaining it.

title: Chromatin-state succession at AP-1 sites after AP-1 loss
description: Profile H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and nucleosome remodeling (BAF/SWI-SNF, p300) at AP-1 sites over time to test whether other factors or epigenetic marks take over the site and persist without AP-1. Combine this with ChIP/CUT&RUN for co-factors and time-resolved AP-1 depletion to see whether the marks outlast AP-1, which would indicate that AP-1 initiates but does not store the memory.

title: Single-cell and lineage-tracing analysis of memory inheritance
description: Use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with barcoded lineages, or live imaging of sister-cell pairs with an AP-1 reporter (e.g., FOS/JUN-driven), to test whether the memory state and AP-1 activity are inherited across divisions and correlated within clones. Compare the heritability of the response with its stability in unrelated cells to distinguish true cellular memory from persistent signaling.

title: Necessity and sufficiency of locus-specific AP-1 binding for memory
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate AP-1 motifs at a few memory-associated enhancers, and use dCas9-based recruitment of JUN/FOS to a naive locus. Test whether a transient pulse of recruitment at that locus alone creates durable accessibility and a stronger re-response. This tests necessity and sufficiency of AP-1 binding for memory at specific loci, as opposed to global signaling effects.

title: Hysteresis after transient stimulus and long washout
description: Expose cells to a brief, defined stimulus (e.g., TPA, serum, or a cytokine pulse) that induces FOS/JUN, then track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene expression for days to weeks after washout. Persistence of accessibility and transcription after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate memory, and a dose-response across pulse strengths would reveal hysteresis.

title: Time-gated AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS/JUN or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 before, during, or after the priming stimulus. If the primed state survives AP-1 removal after the establishment window, AP-1 is only an initiator; if it is lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain the state. Readouts are ATAC-seq, H3K27ac and response to re-stimulation.

title: Single-cell live reporter imaging with lineage tracking
description: Image endogenous AP-1 activity (knock-in FOS/JUN fluorescent tags plus an AP-1 transcriptional reporter) in single cells across stimulation, rest and re-stimulation, tracking daughter cells through divisions. Measure heterogeneity per cell rather than averaging, and test whether past activity history predicts later response amplitude and whether the state is heritable through mitosis, which would indicate a cell-intrinsic, bistable memory.

title: AP-1 motif mutation and remodeler recruitment at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or enhancer deletion to mutate AP-1 motifs at enhancers that remain open after stimulation, then test whether they still gain and retain accessibility, H3K4me1/H3K27ac, and faster re-induction. Pair this with Micro-C or ChIP for BAF/chromatin remodelers to test whether AP-1 recruits remodelers that leave a lasting chromatin change.

title: Second-stimulus response in primed vs. naive cells with mathematical modeling
description: Compare primed and naive cells (in vitro and in vivo, e.g., inflamed vs. naive skin or epithelial stem cells) for the response to a second stimulus using RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and footprinting, then fit a mathematical model (positive feedback, chromatin-state variables) to the data. Perturb predicted feedback components, such as AP-1 autoregulation or histone modifiers, to test whether the model explains persistence and distinguishes AP-1-driven memory from other mechanisms.

title: Intersection of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin state at the same loci
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury), measure two independent readouts at the same loci: AP-1 (FOS/JUN) ChIP/CUT&RUN occupancy and ATAC-seq accessibility or H3K27ac. Loci where both persist long after the stimulus ends, and where AP-1 motif-containing sites are the only overlap, are candidate memory sites.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after the stimulus ends (maintenance necessity test)
description: Prime cells, wash out the stimulus, and after a rest period add a dTAG/AID degron or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 only during the memory phase. Compare accessibility and the faster secondary response on restimulation with controls; loss of memory when AP-1 is removed after induction would show that AP-1 is required to maintain memory, not only to establish it.

title: Sufficiency of optogenetic or chemogenetic AP-1 pulses
description: Drive FOS/JUN activity with a light- or drug-inducible system in naive cells using pulses of different duration and frequency, then measure persistent chromatin opening and altered transcriptional responses to a later unrelated stimulus. This tests whether AP-1 activity alone can establish a lasting state and how its dynamics encode dose or history.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked persistence and heritability of the primed state
description: Use live AP-1 reporters (e.g., FOS-GFP) with time-lapse imaging, or barcoded lineages with scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq, to track whether the primed state passes through cell divisions and for how many generations it lasts. This gives a time-resolved record per cell, showing whether the state is bistable or heritable rather than a decaying signal.

title: Pioneer-like activity and cofactor dependence at primed enhancers
description: Mutate or CRISPR-delete AP-1 motifs at specific primed enhancers, and use CUT&Tag, BAF/SWI-SNF inhibition, and Micro-C to test whether AP-1 recruits remodelers and keeps chromatin loops open. Reporter assays for memory (faster reinduction of the linked gene) will show whether site-specific AP-1 binding is causal, as opposed to alternatives such as other transcription factors or DNA methylation.

title: First-order reversal curves for AP-1 target loci
description: Drive cells with a ramp of AP-1 input (optogenetic or inducible c-Fos/c-Jun, or a defined stimulus dose), reverse the ramp at varied peak levels, then sweep back up. Measure single-cell reporter output (AP-1 activity, chromatin accessibility at target enhancers) to map per-locus up and down thresholds, testing whether hysteresis and bistable switching exist rather than a simple graded response.

title: Return-point and wiping memory with nested stimulus histories
description: Apply stimulus sequences with nested maxima and minima, such as a small excursion inside a larger one, then measure the final chromatin or transcriptional state. Test whether the state depends on the order of extreme amplitudes rather than timing, and whether larger excursions erase the imprint of smaller ones. Return-point memory would support a history-encoding mechanism rather than a transient signal.

title: Decay kinetics of the remembered state
description: After a transient AP-1 pulse, measure accessibility, H3K27ac and target expression over hours to weeks, with and without cell division. Fit logarithmic-in-time versus exponential decay, and use perturbations such as proliferation arrest, temperature, or BET/HDAC inhibitors to distinguish stable self-sustaining memory from slow forgetting (passive dilution or residual signaling).

title: Staged AP-1 removal after priming with dominant-negative and degron perturbations
description: At staged times after the priming stimulus, acutely remove AP-1 (A-Fos dominant negative, or dTAG/auxin degron on c-Jun/FOSL) and measure ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN and RNA output. If memory persists after AP-1 loss, it is stored elsewhere; if it is lost, it requires continuous AP-1. Varying the priming time tests whether AP-1 carries the memory or only establishes it.

title: Re-stimulation response test against naive cells
description: Prime cells with a known stimulus, rest them, then re-challenge with a standard test dose and compare with naive cells.
