Measure induction speed and magnitude, AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN) and accessibility at primed sites, and whether the effect scales with prior dose. Matched naive controls and different priming doses allow the memory signal to be calibrated and separated from later effects such as secondary signalling.

title: Hysteresis in the AP-1 dose-response
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or PMA/ERK input driving FOS/JUN) up and then down in single cells, and measure AP-1 activity and target-gene output (live reporters, chromatin accessibility) to determine whether the descending branch differs from the ascending one. A gap that persists after long waits and decays logarithmically rather than exponentially would indicate stable memory with many energy barriers rather than slow relaxation.

title: Decay kinetics of AP-1 memory and erasure by decaying pulses or degradation
description: After a transient stimulus, measure AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene expression over days to weeks to determine decay kinetics. Then attempt to erase the memory with an oscillating stimulus of decreasing amplitude or by acute degron-mediated removal of AP-1, to test whether AP-1 is needed for maintenance and not only for initiation.

title: First-order reversal curve analysis of AP-1 sites
description: Apply stimulus histories with different peak and reversal levels, then measure accessibility or reporter activity at individual AP-1 enhancers. Fit a Preisach-type model with two thresholds per site to obtain the distribution of switching thresholds, and test return-point memory by cycling partway, returning, and checking whether the state is retraced exactly. This shows whether memory resides in independent enhancer switches or in their coupling.

title: Order-of-exposure experiments to resolve layered memory
description: Expose cells to sequential stimuli (e.g., wounding, then inflammation, then a third signal) in different orders. Use time-resolved ATAC/CUT&Tag to determine whether later AP-1 events overwrite or add to earlier accessible sites, and use stepwise degron depletion to remove layers successively. This tests whether the memory is hierarchical and which earlier imprints a later stimulus can overwrite.

title: Distinguishing site-intrinsic from network-based memory by perturbing cooperativity
description: Separate the contribution of individual AP-1 motifs from that of the surrounding network (positive feedback of FOS/JUN on its own promoters, cooperation with partner factors such as ETS or the SWI/SNF complex). Mutate motifs at single enhancers by CRISPR and block feedback loops or chromatin remodelers, then measure single-cell bistability and persistence of the primed state. If memory is lost when coupling is cut but not when motifs are retained, memory is a network property rather than a property of individual sites.

title: Sweep-rate and relaxation controls for AP-1 hysteresis
description: Stimulate cells with graded, ramped doses of a signal (e.g., TPA, EGF, or anisomycin) up and down at several sweep rates, then measure AP-1 activity (FOS/JUN levels, a reporter, ATAC accessibility at AP-1 motifs). If hysteresis loop width shrinks as the sweep slows, the apparent memory is slow relaxation; if it persists at slow rates, it reflects a bistable or stored state. Repeat the sweep in a JUN/FOS degradation-rate mutant to separate slow kinetics from true retention.

title: First-order reversal curve mapping of single-cell AP-1 thresholds
description: Drive cells partway up the dose axis, reverse, and repeat from many reversal points. Use live single-cell AP-1 reporters or multiplexed imaging to build a Preisach-type distribution of up- and down-switching thresholds across cells. A population of bistable cells with distinct thresholds would support a memory composed of many two-state units, while a unimodal graded response would argue against it.

title: Return-point memory and erasure with decaying-oscillation stimulation
description: Give a pulse history with a defined peak and vary the stimulus within that peak, then test whether AP-1 target gene output and chromatin state retain only the maximum (return-point memory). Test erasure with a slowly decaying oscillating stimulus or an inhibitor washout (e.g., dominant-negative FOS such as A-FOS), and measure how much stimulus is needed to erase the record. Compare the dose needed to erase with the dose needed to establish it.

title: Locating memory sites by AP-1 binding, chromatin state, and motif mutation
description: Map FOS/JUN binding (CUT&RUN or ChIP), accessibility (ATAC-seq), and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at enhancer sites before, during, and after the stimulus. Then mutate individual AP-1 motifs with CRISPR or degrade AP-1 with a degron after the stimulus, and test whether enhancer accessibility and the response to a second stimulus persist without AP-1. This distinguishes memory held in AP-1 itself, in feedback loops, or in chromatin sites that AP-1 only opened.

title: Interval, cell division and interruption effects on memory stability
description: Vary the interval between the first and second stimulus (minutes to weeks) and the number of cell divisions between them, and use single-cell tracking to test whether the second response is primed. Insert interruptions (e.g., a temporary signaling block mid-history) to test whether they are reflected as reduced later responses. Fit the decay to extract a retention half-life and an energy-barrier-like stability parameter, to determine whether AP-1 memory lasts hours, days or generations.

title: First-order reversal curve stimulation protocols
description: Drive cells to saturating AP-1 activation (e.g., high-dose TPA or serum/MAPK stimulation), withdraw to varied reversal levels, then re-stimulate, and read out chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene transcription at each step. Identify which AP-1 sites and genes show path-dependent responses with return-point memory versus simple relaxation, to identify a history-dependent, hysteresis-like state and distinguish it from the effect of stimulus level alone.

title: Pause experiments with decay time series
description: Give a stimulus, pause or wash out for different durations, then restimulate and compare the response with naive cells, tracking FOS/JUN levels, AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), and enhancer accessibility over time. If the primed response persists long after AP-1 protein levels return to baseline, and the persistence is distinguishable from slow relaxation by varying pause length and temperature, memory is more than a lingering transient.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics across repeated stimulation
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN reporters and an AP-1 transcriptional reporter in single cells across repeated stimulations, resolving discrete bursts and enhancer switching events. Analyze the distribution of switching thresholds across cells and test for bistability using a Preisach-type decomposition into independent two-state loci, each with its own on and off thresholds.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation with erasure controls
description: Use degron-tagged or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 at defined times: during priming, during the memory interval, or only at restimulation. Compare with erasure controls such as a decaying oscillating stimulus, and read out chromatin state and gene expression. If AP-1 is needed only to write the memory, it is an initiator; if removal during the interval erases the memory, it is a maintainer.

title: Site-specific mutation and epigenetic readout of pioneer-like AP-1 sites
description: Edit individual AP-1 motifs in memory-associated enhancers with CRISPR, or block them with dCas9, and measure whether priming-induced accessibility, H3K27ac, and enhanced re-induction are lost, using ATAC-seq, ChIP/CUT&Tag for histone marks and SWI/SNF (BAF), and nascent RNA. Combine this with a chromatin-state perturbation, such as a BAF inhibitor, to test whether the stored state is a self-sustaining chromatin state or only slow relaxation of AP-1 itself.

title: Rate-independent hysteresis of AP-1 target output
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or chemically induced ERK/JNK activation, or serum) up and down at progressively slower rates, and measure c-Fos/c-Jun levels, chromatin accessibility, and target-gene transcription in single cells. A hysteresis loop that persists in the quasi-static limit would indicate rate-independent memory rather than kinetic lag from slow protein or mRNA turnover, and a lag-only model can be fitted and rejected.

title: Return-point memory by nested stimulus amplitude sequences
description: Drive cells with nested sequences of stimulus amplitudes (up to A1, down to B1, up to A2<A1, and so on) and measure AP-1 occupancy and reporter activity at each turning point. If the system retains the earlier extrema in nested fashion and a larger excursion erases the smaller ones, this supports a Preisach-like population of AP-1 sites with distinct thresholds, as opposed to a single global state variable.

title: Preisach-type decomposition of AP-1 enhancers from single-cell multiome data
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN, and RNA-seq after stimulation at graded doses and durations to estimate each enhancer's on and off thresholds, then test whether the population response is reproduced by a distribution of independent bistable switches. Sites that open at a high threshold and close only at a much lower one would be the memory elements, and a model built from these thresholds can be used to predict held-out stimulus histories.

title: Amplitude-memory training, readout, and erasure tests
description: Train cells with repeated pulses at a defined amplitude or frequency, rest them for varying times, then probe with a test stimulus to see whether the response depends on the training amplitude (Keim–Nagel protocol). Compare a single probe with repeated probes to test whether reading is destructive. Test erasure by A-FOS (AP-1 dominant-negative) expression, cell division, or a pulse larger than the trained one, and test whether the memory depends on chromatin remodeling by perturbing SWI/SNF or histone modifiers.

title: Non-monotonic relaxation after a perturbation to test for hidden state variables
description: Apply a step change in stimulus or signaling, such as a transient JNK/ERK inhibitor or activator pulse, and track AP-1 activity and chromatin state as they relax. Compare the trajectories of two preparations that reach the same instantaneous AP-1 level through different histories; different later relaxation, such as non-monotonic overshoot, would show that the cell carries hidden state variables beyond AP-1 level, for example chromatin accessibility or partner-factor composition. Perturbing these hidden variables can then distinguish a switch-like mechanism from a phase-like one.

title: Graded perturbation of candidate AP-1 memory carriers
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, EGF, or TPA), progressively remove candidate memory carriers in graded steps: titrate dominant-negative FOS (A-FOS), deplete FOS/JUN by degron, then inhibit chromatin remodelers (BAF) or histone writers. Measure ATAC-seq accessibility and re-stimulation response after each step. A single monotonic decay to baseline implies one mechanism, while a change in slope implies multiple layers, for example a fast AP-1 protein-dependent component and a slow chromatin-based one.

title: Acute versus persistent AP-1 occupancy time course
description: Perform CUT&RUN/ChIP for FOS/JUN family members, ATAC-seq, and H3K27ac at multiple times after stimulus withdrawal (hours to weeks). This distinguishes sites where AP-1 itself persists, sites where accessibility persists after AP-1 is gone, and sites that fully revert, and the decay time course dates each memory.

title: First-order reversal curve mapping of response thresholds
description: Subject cells to defined sequences of stimulus dose increases and decreases (minor loops with varied reversal points), and read out single-cell AP-1 reporter activity and target gene transcription. Fit a Preisach-type model of independent bistable units, each locus or cell having its own switching threshold, to test for hysteresis and return-point memory, and compare threshold distributions with and without AP-1 perturbation to determine whether AP-1 sets the hysteresis.

title: Dependence of memory on priming-challenge interval and priming duration
description: Vary the time between the priming stimulus and the challenge, and the duration of priming, in fibroblasts, keratinocytes, or macrophages. Measure whether the magnitude or kinetics of the secondary response depends on the interval and scales with priming dose and duration. Pair this with live imaging of an AP-1 reporter and single-cell lineage tracking to test whether memory is inherited through division.

title: Causality controls using timing, clonal comparison, and motif mutagenesis
description: Deliver optogenetic or inducible AP-1 pulses before versus after a separate chromatin-altering event (e.g., differentiation signal or inflammatory challenge) to test whether AP-1-dependent accessibility precedes or follows it. Also compare AP-1 motif sites across cell clones with independent priming histories: shared sites would suggest a deterministic imprint, whereas clone-specific, random sites would suggest the signal arose later. Complement this with CRISPR motif mutagenesis at selected enhancers to test necessity for the remembered response.

title: Sweep-rate dependence of hysteresis in AP-1 target accessibility
description: Drive cells with a ramped up-and-down stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or PMA/ERK input controlling FOS/JUN) at several sweep rates, and measure ATAC-seq accessibility or reporter output at AP-1 target loci. Memory is defined as the rate-independent hysteresis loop area that persists as sweeps slow, which distinguishes true bistable/epigenetic hysteresis from slow relaxation kinetics.

title: First-order reversal curves of single-cell AP-1 thresholds
description: Saturate AP-1 activity, reverse to varied intermediate input levels, then increase the input again while reading single-cell reporters of AP-1 targets. The resulting first-order reversal curve map gives the distribution of up- and down-switching thresholds across cells or loci, testing whether the system consists of bistable units with return-point memory.

title: Return-point memory test with nested stimulus histories
description: Apply stimulus histories with nested peaks and reversals of different amplitudes, such as serial pulses of varying strength. Test whether AP-1 binding and chromatin state retain only the extreme values of the history and not intermediate ones. Compare ChIP/CUT&RUN and transcriptional readouts across history orderings to show history-dependence beyond the current input.

title: Erasure assays with AP-1 perturbation
description: After priming, erase memory at different times by applying decaying oscillations of input, dominant-negative AP-1 (A-Fos), or degron-mediated depletion. Measure how completely accessibility and primed transcriptional responses on restimulation are lost, and whether defects persist partially, to show whether AP-1 is required for maintenance and not only for establishment.

title: Analysis of persistent AP-1 sites, single-locus switching events, and pause-resume protocol
description: Map AP-1 motifs and bound sites that remain accessible after stimulus removal and mutate them by CRISPR to test whether memory is lost locally. Additionally, record single-locus live imaging or nascent transcription bursts to detect discrete switching events, and use a pause-then-resume stimulation protocol to test whether a transient exposure leaves a latent, recoverable signature on reactivation.

title: Long-timescale decay assay of AP-1 memory
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or anisomycin) is removed, measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy by CUT&RUN, chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq, and target transcription over hours to weeks. Fit decay curves to distinguish true persistence from slow transients, and test whether the decay time depends on dose, duration or cell division.

title: Stimulus-history mapping with reversal and return doses
description: Expose cells to a series of stimulus doses that rise and then reverse, varying the peak (reversal) dose and the return dose, and read out single-cell AP-1 activity with a live reporter and downstream gene expression. The resulting two-dimensional response map shows whether subpopulations behave as hysteretic switches with distinct thresholds and biases, and whether the response depends on history beyond the current dose.

title: Return-point memory test with nested stimulus cycles and decaying-amplitude erasure
description: Apply a major stimulus loop, then a minor sub-cycle inside it, and test whether accessibility at AP-1 sites and gene output return exactly to the state at the turning point. Compare this with a decaying-amplitude oscillating stimulus protocol, which would erase the memory if it is stored in AP-1-dependent chromatin states.

title: Separating AP-1 from the chromatin sites it marks
description: Acutely degrade FOS/JUN (dTAG/auxin) after stimulation and measure whether accessibility and enhancer marks (H3K27ac) persist, which would place memory in the chromatin state rather than in AP-1 itself. Complement this with mutation or CRISPR deletion of individual AP-1 motifs and with pioneer-factor tests (e.g., BAF nucleosome remodeling) to identify which sites are self-sustaining.

title: Re-stimulation test of whether the same sites reactivate
description: Restimulate cells after a rest period and use single-cell multiome (scATAC and RNA) to test whether the same loci open faster or more strongly in the same cells compared with naive cells. Add lineage tracing or sibling-cell pairing to test inheritance through division, and compare naive versus primed cells with AP-1 dominant-negative (A-FOS) to test necessity.
